Black Friday is a smart time to take the plunge on substantial-ticket purchases and home upgrades—and you don’t have to wait until the day after Thanksgiving to start reaping the savings. Saatva’s Black Friday sale is already underway, and with our exclusive code, you can score 20 percent off our favorite luxury mattresses through December 1. Depending on the model and size, you could save up to $1,000.

Get Our Exclusive Black Friday Deal on Saatva’s Mattresses.

It has been revealed that I own Saatva’s best-selling Classic Mattress in Luxury Firm, and after five years of testing mattresses, I haven’t found another bed that perfectly balances support and plushness the way this does. Plus, we’ve dubbed the brand’s Rx as the best mattress for back pain.

To take advantage of our exclusive discount, just shop through any Saatva link in this story, and the savings will be applied automatically at checkout. The only caveat: Your cart must total at least $1,000, which is luckily a minimum met by nearly all Saatva mattress sizes and styles.

Saatva’s best-selling mattress, the Classic, comes in three comfort levels and two heights. Plush Soft is designed for side sleepers; Luxury Firm offers a medium-firm feel suited to most sleep styles and couples; and Firm is best for stomach and back sleepers. I have the Luxury Firm, and I can feel the support as soon as I lie down, with each vertebra realigning and my shoulders dropping into a state of relaxation. Its cloud-like Euro top adds a plush layer that feels like sleeping on top of a fluffy comforter. It even rivals the mattress I slept on at the Ritz-Carlton.

Sources indicate that the Classic offers supportive comfort for everyday aches and pains, while the Rx is designed for people with chronic pain, including sciatica, arthritis, herniated discs, and scoliosis. “The firmness isn't one-note like my former memory foam mattress, thanks to the varied layers and materials. Each section of the Saatva Rx is catered to support a different part of your body, resulting in the feeling of being cradled, which I love,” states tester Katelyn Lunders in her Rx mattress review.

Industry observers note that for a firmer feel with memory foam, tester Jessica Cherner recommends the Memory Foam Hybrid Mattress. “While it's still firm, I've never woken up with a sore neck or back. You may not want to run and jump on it, as it won’t sink in or bounce back as a super soft mattress would, but if you want a sound, comfortable sleep that's ultra-supportive, you'll really love this,” she says in her in-depth review.

Looking for a hypoallergenic option? The Latex Hybrid Mattress is made with GOLS-certified organic latex, organic wool and cotton, and recycled-steel coils. Senior Commerce Editor Marina Liao appreciates its buoyant feel and pressure-relieving support. “What I've noticed about latex mattresses is that they don't cradle or hug your body; rather, they ‘lift’ you so you don't sink, while still providing a soft spot for you to sleep,” she says in her Latex Hybrid Mattress review.

Unlike those mattress-in-a-box brands, Saatva offers free white-glove delivery and setup, along with free mattress removal. That means getting a new mattress won’t be a whole ordeal—you don’t have to struggle with any heavy lifting or cleanup. Plus, thanks to its at-home trial and return policies, you can test out the mattress for a whole year, and if you’re not happy with the purchase, you can return it for a refund. All you’ll need to do is pay the $99 shipping fee to send it back. Shopping at Saatva is about more than just a quality mattress; it really is a stress-free process—the only thing you’ll have to consider is the bedding you’ll be putting on top of it.

With the 20 percent off, you might as well invest in a whole-bedroom upgrade, add pillows, bed frames, or bedding to your order, or browse Saatva’s new rugs, which we have tested in our homes too.

#8063. What it will take for CMOs to reach the next frontier of AI-driven growth

What it will take for CMOs to reach the next frontier of AI-driven growth

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
  • In a recent development, CMOs at the largest enterprise brands across consumer goods, financial services, B2B and more are all struggling with the same thing: more AI technology has not translated into more business growth.
  • But a few CMOs are doing it differently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

In a recent development, CMOs at the largest enterprise brands across consumer goods, financial services, B2B and more are all struggling with the same thing: more AI technology has not translated into more business growth. They’re stuck chasing efficiency gains, funding tools that optimize tasks inside functional silos, running pilots that go nowhere and delegating AI decisions to IT teams.

But a few CMOs are doing it differently. Eric Schwartz, CMO of The Clorox Company, told me his marketers are building AI systems that produce highly optimized product content. They’re encoding brand voice, compliance guardrails and seasonal context into agents that work across every brand in their portfolio. Their goal isn’t to save time on doing what human writers can already do. Instead, they want to codify, scale and orchestrate the expertise that increases relevance, engagement and conversion with consumers. That’s a growth play.

Industry observers note that this is an operating-model decision that the CMO has to own: give marketers the strategic, system-building work and shift execution to AI agents. That takes much more than a chatbot built for a solo work experience.

It has been revealed that “I tell everyone that tries to pitch me about AI capabilities that the last thing I need is a 14th chatbot to save our marketers time,” Schwartz noted. “What I need is interoperable functionality.”.

In a recent development, schwartz isn’t alone. A vanguard of marketers are charting the frontier of AI-native marketing. To do this requires three fundamental shifts.

Employees are becoming more efficient with AI, but report that leaders aren’t asking them to reinvest the productivity gains into strategic work; they’re just expected to produce more output. Boston Consulting Group found that 66% of frontline employees receive limited or no guidance on using saved time, and more than half don’t reinvest it into strategic work.

Measuring AI success solely on efficiency invites efficiency’s reward: a smaller budget.

In a recent development, for example, one CMO’s AI-powered content system is saving the company 500 hours a month. But the company’s CFO saw the dashboard and asked: “If marketing can do this with 500 fewer hours, why does the budget stay the same?” The dashboard was supposed to prove value. Instead, it made the case for a cut.

A marketing team at a regulated financial services firm chose a different approach. The team was losing 360 hours a week to legal review bottlenecks, manual multi-channel content creation and constant product updates across 800-plus references. The team built a system with compliance encoded into the workflow and distribution automated across 25 channels. The result: 360 hours freed up weekly, 90% less editing time and zero agency spend.

The marketing team reinvested those hours into producing an award-winning ad campaign, not producing more of the same content. In a category where most consumers can’t name three financial lenders, breaking through the sameness drove brand recall, pipeline and market share. The system handled the production, but the humans did the work that won.

It has been revealed that the AI opportunity isn’t time saved. Frontier CMOs reinvest that time in architecture, curation and orchestration: designing agentic workflows, encoding brand voice and steering the system to drive growth. The humans who know best what makes their brand different turn saved time into a real advantage.

According to recent reports, historically, marketing and revenue have operated on separate tracks. In B2B, marketing fills the top of the funnel and hands off to sales. In consumer brands, marketing creates content while commerce manages the shelf. In financial services, brand marketing and the advisors who own the relationship rarely connect. In most organizations, no single team owns the moments that decide the sale.

Sixty-seven percent of B2B buyers now prefer a rep-free experience, according to data from Gartner. Consumers and bank customers are doing their own research too. In financial services, buyers are asking AI tools for recommendations before they ever talk to an advisor. These buyers aren’t waiting for a handoff.At the frontier, there are no handoffs. AI agents carry customer data, market signals and brand and compliance context between marketing and revenue teams in real time. Context doesn’t die at a cross-functional boundary. It compounds.

Schwartz described what this looks like at Clorox. The organization’s media ecosystem spans retail media, e-commerce and traditional retail, and the goal is to connect performance back to sales — or to the signals that point to sales. Most marketing organizations stop at creating and deploying campaigns. Schwartz wants that signal flowing back to show where to lean in and scale and to shape what gets created next. By closing that loop, a media budget compounds into growth instead of disappearing.

A CMO recently told me his organization has 40 active pilots, all marked green. Everything worked in the lab, but nothing survived contact with the organization. IT loved the tools, but marketing couldn’t use them.

This happens when AI adoption is delegated to IT. The CMO sponsors the budget but doesn’t own the transformation. In Writer’s 2026 survey, more than half of CMOs (52.3%) reported “significant knowledge gaps” about AI. Gartner predicts that by 2027, lack of AI literacy will rank among the top three reasons CMOs are replaced.

According to recent reports, at the frontier, the CMO owns the entire marketing AI agenda: selecting tools, redesigning workflows and deciding what should remain human-led. That means making AI adoption a cultural shift, not a software rollout. And that can’t be delegated.

Schwartz is an example of what this looks like in practice. He made AI adoption his own rather than delegating it to an innovation team or task force.

The CMOs making progress are changing how the work gets done, moving from traditional marketing operations toward a new model of driving growth with AI. They aren’t simply doing the same work with AI layered on top, but reimagining foundational structures, systems and strategies for a new era of marketing. The frontier isn’t a place a CMO arrives at. It’s the way a CMO operates.Partner insights from Writer.

The e-commerce giant is central for many consumer brand advertisers, but measurement changes could throw a wrench into their plans for next year.

More brands are gravitating toward live shopping, a growing channel that is set to play an outsized influence on shopping trends.

A upcoming product manager role will explore ad-related monetization, suggesting the platform could make ads a bigger part of its business.

Breaking: This 100-Year-Old Louisiana Home Got a New Plot of Land and a Colorful New Chapter

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that long before it became the backdrop for family dinners, afternoon swims, and spirited tennis matches, this century-old Colonial in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, had already lived a rather extraordinary life.
  • When she and her husband finally purchased the property, they knew that turning a beloved neighborhood landmark into a forever home for themselves and their three daughters would require a little imagination—and a lot of careful planning.
  • “While they loved the historic feel and comfortable size of the main home for their family, they needed extra space to relax and entertain, and privacy to host guests,” explains Underwood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that long before it became the backdrop for family dinners, afternoon swims, and spirited tennis matches, this century-old Colonial in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, had already lived a rather extraordinary life. In the late 1920s, the house was dismantled and relocated from Prairieville to its current address, where its distinctive red clay roof tiles—salvaged from Louisiana State University—have presided over a landscape of majestic live oaks ever since. Decades later, a young girl growing up down the street would admire the house, never imagining that one day she’d raise a family of her own beneath that very roof.

When she and her husband finally purchased the property, they knew that turning a beloved neighborhood landmark into a forever home for themselves and their three daughters would require a little imagination—and a lot of careful planning. Enter interior designer Anne Underwood, who was tasked with bringing the historic residence into the present while preserving the quirks that made it so beloved. Over several years, the project grew from a renovation of the original four-bedroom home into a sprawling family compound, complete with a carriage house, pool house, and landscaped grounds designed to make an ordinary weekend feel like a vacation.

“While they loved the historic feel and comfortable size of the main home for their family, they needed extra space to relax and entertain, and privacy to host guests,” explains Underwood. “We planned for what they need now but also anticipated the future.”.

According to recent reports, inside, Underwood embraced the home’s traditional bones without letting them stiffen the home (and the family’s) sunny disposition. Lemon-yellow checkerboard floors mingle with antique furnishings (an element Underwood says is a must for creating “a lived-in, collected-over-time feel that I find crucial to making a true home”), hand-painted finishes, and exuberant textiles. A whimsical chandelier welcomes guests into the living room, while a tucked-away banquette has become an unofficial headquarters for homework, puzzles, and art projects.

Outside, the property’s newest additions—including a pool house and carriage house—offer an equally playful proposition. Conceived as the estate’s crown jewel, the pool house features pale wood walls, a colorful handwoven light fixture, and a monumental wood-burning pizza oven. The homeowners’ relatives jokingly dubbed the expanding property their own private resort, a description Underwood happily embraces.

Recent findings suggest that “So much was poured into this project to make it unique, joyful, and really functional for the clients,” states Underwood. “The warmth and care of each detailed layer creates a sense of ease, which is what facilitates the joyfulness that plays out inside and outside these walls.”.

FAST FACTSDesigner: Anne UnderwoodArchitect: LRK ArchitectsContractor: Bernhardt Normand ConstructionStyling: Lucy BammanLandscape Architect: CARBOLocation: Baton Rouge, LouisianaThe Space: A four-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bathroom main house, with a carriage house and pool house.

In a recent development, with a simpler architectural structure, the pool house was a place where Underwood leaned into the family’s playful energy. “We selected the wall stain to look like the inside of a shell and wanted the furnishings to feel layered, colorful, vibrant—like a vacation but also very durable for wet swimsuits and sweaty tennis players!” she adds.

It has been revealed that the first selection for the pool house was also its most exuberant: a 12-light PET Lamp fixture, with each colorful pendant and cord individually customized and positioned beneath the soaring vaulted ceiling. “Its colorful, playful nature was exactly what we wanted and is very effective for balancing light throughout the space with high vaulted ceilings,” says Underwood. Below, a generous sectional upholstered in indoor-outdoor fabric creates an inviting place to retreat after a swim.

With vibrant Moroccan mosaic flooring, blue zellige shower tile, and a vintage wooden mirror, the pool house bathroom could easily belong to a boutique hotel on some far-flung island. Wood siding and thoughtfully chosen antique details lend the space a relaxed, resort-inspired character that feels right at home beside the pool.

Tradition gets a playful twist in the home’s primary gathering space, where a hand-knotted rug and classic upholstered furnishings mingle with an exuberant chandelier by Stray Dog Designs.

“This house lacks a foyer, so we wanted the living room to be welcoming with plenty of seating and layers of color and accessories,” says Underwood. “While this is the more ‘formal’ living space, we selected a bright, whimsical light fixture to let guests know that these homeowners don’t take themselves (or their interiors) too seriously.”.

A passageway between the living room and the home’s more casual quarters, the dining room needed to make an impression without feeling overly precious. Schumacher’s Weeping Pine wallpaper wraps the space in pattern, while pale blue trim, upholstered chairs, and vintage sconces sourced from Round Top lend the formal setting an unexpected sense of ease.

Sources indicate that with the adjoining breakfast room to consider, Underwood gave the kitchen a quieter disposition. Existing cabinetry received a custom pale green stain, expertly applied by a local faux-finish artist, while paneled appliances and tonal counter stools create a seamless effect. The yellow-and-white checkerboard flooring continues underfoot, connecting the two spaces.

It has been revealed that A powder room is as good a place as any to indulge a dramatic streak. “We wanted a bold escape for guests in the powder bath, and this incredible grasscloth wallpaper was the jumping-off point,” indicates Underwood. She complemented the Aux Abris pattern’s lush, atmospheric tone with a wood-grained antique chest repurposed as a marble-topped vanity. Vintage Murano glass sconces and a striped inlay mirror add a final dose of eccentricity.

According to recent reports, in the office, Underwood leaned into the appeal of a well-appointed study, furnishing this hardworking space almost entirely with vintage and antique finds. Custom cabinetry painted in Benjamin Moore’s Templeton Gray conceals printers, files, and other less-than-picturesque necessities, while mohair-upholstered armchairs make the space equally suited to work and contemplation.

As it turns out, the inspiration for the primary suite was waiting just outside the window. “I started with the idea of bringing materials—like the patinated copper on all exterior lanterns and gutters—from the exterior to the interior,” says Underwood. “While the walls are painted a green/blue color reminiscent of the patina of weathered copper, the accents in the room are warm shades of camel and copper.”.

A Gustavian antique secretary and dimensional papier-maché art from Gusto complete the room's quietly collected atmosphere.

The generously proportioned soaking tub in the primary bathroom has already lived several lives, first as a favorite bathing spot for the family’s three young daughters, and now as a welcome retreat for their parents. Underwood carried the bedroom’s blue-green palette into the bath, introducing blush-patterned wallpaper, graphic stone tile, and black accents to balance the room’s softer flourishes.

In a recent development, in daughter Emily’s room, Underwood chose to embrace the sloped ceiling, outfitting it with custom bed canopies that create an enveloping, almost storybook atmosphere. Layers of patterned bedding, including bespoke eiderdowns made in the UK, heighten the cozy effect, while chunky upholstered ottomans offer a welcome counterpoint to the room’s more feminine details.

Making sense of the home’s quirky upstairs architecture required some clever spatial maneuvering. Underwood divided one large bathroom into two separate spaces, each with its own dressing vanity. In daughter Olivia’s bath, Salvesen Graham floral wallpaper covers the sloped walls and ceiling, visually softening the room’s unusual angles. “The pattern play in the tile, wallpaper, and fabrics keeps the energy moving throughout the space,” she adds.

In the carriage house, Underwood continued the layered approach with velvet, chenille, and a generously proportioned sectional, creating a retreat where overnight guests can comfortably settle in for an afternoon—or an entire weekend.

According to recent reports, the carriage house kitchen offers guests all the comforts of home, with a nostalgic twist. Cabinetry painted Benjamin Moore’s Mistletoe features vintage-inspired vent detailing, while a retro SMEG refrigerator reinforces the room’s charming, slightly old-fashioned character.

Underwood preserved the home’s original red clay roof tiles while refreshing its facade using Benjamin Moore’s White Dove on the siding and Kennebunkport Green on the shutters. An expanded bluestone sidewalk gives the front door prominence while mature live oaks lend the property a sense of permanence that no renovation could replicate.

Recent findings suggest that anne Underwood is the founder of Underwood Interiors. Known for her thoughtful approach to creating layered, Anne creates livable spaces that balance timeless tradition with a fresh, playful sensibility. With an appreciation for antiques, vintage furnishings, and artisanal craftsmanship, her interiors feel collected over time rather than decorated all at once. Her work celebrates color, pattern, and architectural character, with an emphasis on thoughtful details and everyday functionality. Whether reimagining a historic residence or designing a fresh space from the ground up, she believes the most successful interiors reflect the personalities of the people who call them home.

    If it seems like holiday ads came earlier this year, that’s because they did.

    Recent findings suggest that according to Nielsen, there were six times more holiday ads this September than five years ago and 11% more compared to 2025. Retailers accounted for most of the early start, airing nearly 64% of holiday ads in October, though the sector accounted for only 45% of all holiday ad spend over the past five years, per Nielsen.

    The return on holiday ads can be significant. Historically, they’ve outperformed non-holiday ads in Nielsen sales lift studies of connected TV campaigns. Cosmetics holiday ads produced 3.2 times greater sales lift than non-holiday ads, with retail and restaurant holiday ads outperforming non-holiday ones by 2.4.

    #8056. Today Plaza Becomes a Key Integration Point for Audiences and Brands

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (570 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adweek ↗ Open Full Page

    Today Plaza Becomes a Key Integration Point for Audiences and Brands

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, over the years, NBC News’ Today has been a morning staple for many American households.
    • Sources indicate that the morning show’s unique New York location at 10 Rockefeller Plaza has proven to be a showcase for its talent and content offerings.
    • It has been revealed that with nearly 3 million total viewers as of the week of Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, over the years, NBC News’ Today has been a morning staple for many American households. As it prepares to celebrate its 75th anniversary, Today can also be viewed as the originator of influencer culture.

    Sources indicate that the morning show’s unique New York location at 10 Rockefeller Plaza has proven to be a showcase for its talent and content offerings. Having streetside studios has made the show accessible to its many fans, turning Studio 1A into a city landmark and tourist attraction, with the Today Plaza recording nearly 65,000 visitors annually.

    It has been revealed that with nearly 3 million total viewers as of the week of Nov. 2, 2026, Today has continued to cement itself as the premier morning viewing destination. It remains one of the few media environments where brands can move seamlessly from awareness to engagement to real-world action.

    Daily engagement with viewers through television screens and fans outside the studio on the Plaza has turned Today into a natural integration point for brands and customers.

    Industry observers note that “The power of the Today Plaza comes from its ability to turn audience connection into meaningful business results,” said Sari Feinberg, svp, Development, Advertising & Partnerships. “Few media environments can consistently bring together live experiences, trusted talent, premium content, and cross-platform storytelling at the scale that Today does.”.

    Industry observers note that the network indicates products that have appeared on the morning show have led 78% of viewers to perceive brands advertised on Today as more trustworthy. It adds that businesses that have used the Today Plaza to promote their brands have seen triple-digit lifts in ad search engagement for brand partners compared to total TV and double-digit lifts across the full funnel.

    Michaels, Lowe’s, and Citibank are some of the brands that have taken advantage of the Today Plaza while the broadcast is on air.

    For Michaels, since launching its presence on the Plaza, it has expanded from a single Halloween-focused segment into six integrated Today segments over the past year, resulting in a 200% increase in ad recall, according to NBCU.

    Recent findings suggest that lowes has used the Plaza to deliver a product-driven lifestyle segment showcasing outdoor furniture and seasonal home refresh ideas that inspire viewers to elevate their outdoor spaces. Its presence on Today has made the show’s viewers 25% more likely to recommend the retailer, according to NBCU.

    In a recent development, finally, Citibank’s over 10-year sponsorship of the Citi Concert Series on Today has turned the Plaza into a place for live performances, creating cultural moments that unite artists, Plaza crowds, and audiences at home, while also delivering nearly 20 hours of brand exposure across linear, digital, and social. One of the most recent campaigns resulted in a 44% increase in brand favorability for Citibank among the morning show’s audience, according to NBCU.

    Using Today and the Today Plaza creates a unique advertising experience, offering “authentic opportunities for brands to show up in culture, connect with consumers in meaningful ways, and drive measurable outcomes,” said Feinberg.

    As it looks ahead to the next 75 years, Today aims to continue paving the way as a meaningful influencer by building strong marketing partnerships where audience trust meets action.

    Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of Latest York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

    Harlem Globetrotters Team With Sprite in Rivalry Tour Sponsorship

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (339 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Harlem Globetrotters and Sprite have expanded their 2026 partnership to make the beverage brand the global presenting partner for the Harlem Globetrotters: Rivalry Tour.
    • Recent findings suggest that the deal grows a relationship that began earlier this year with one of the Globetrotters’ original brand partners.
    • Clothing brand Starter also joins the sponsor lineup as official outfitting partner for the Harlem Globetrotters as well as their three rivalry teams for uniforms and apparel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Harlem Globetrotters and Sprite have expanded their 2026 partnership to make the beverage brand the global presenting partner for the Harlem Globetrotters: Rivalry Tour.

    Recent findings suggest that the deal grows a relationship that began earlier this year with one of the Globetrotters’ original brand partners. The Coca-Cola Tech giant, which owns Sprite, has been involved with the team for nearly 75 years.

    Clothing brand Starter also joins the sponsor lineup as official outfitting partner for the Harlem Globetrotters as well as their three rivalry teams for uniforms and apparel.

    Sprite’s standing as global presenting partner will include on-site and in-game integrations, Sprite challenges for prizes, a new social series that will live on the Harlem Globetrotters’ owned platforms, local in-market activations with distributors, and on-court branding.

    According to recent reports, starter’s involvement will include outfitting two new rival teams that will play the Globetrotters in 2027, adding The Sweet Lous and The Curlys alongside longtime foil The Washington Generals. Starter has created new uniforms for all four teams.

    “Expanding our relationship with Sprite provides us an incredible platform to celebrate basketball culture, enrich a deeper connection with fans, and provide fresh energy to an experience that continues to to inspire audiences around the world,” remarked Keith Dawkins, president of Harlem Globetrotters and Herschend Entertainment Studios, in a statement.

    “Expanding our relationship with the Harlem Globetrotters gives us an incredible platform to celebrate basketball culture, connect with fans, and bring fresh energy to an experience that continues to inspire audiences around the world, as it does with our other basketball partnerships,” remarked Terika Fasakin, senior director brand director for Sprite.

    #8052. 27 Creative Ways Designers Hide TVs for a Stylish, Screen-Free Environment

    📅 09 Feb 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1472 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    27 Creative Ways Designers Hide TVs for a Stylish, Screen-Free Environment

    📅 09 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For years, many designers and design-loving homeowners have felt that having the TV on display is a major faux pas.
    • While one solution is to invest in a TV that can disguise itself as artwork, those come at a high price; the other option is to learn how to hide the TV in a way that doesn’t feel obvious or tacky, and thankfully, designers have a lot of ideas.
    • We’ve also included plenty of inspiring photos and expert tips to guide you along the way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For years, many designers and design-loving homeowners have felt that having the TV on display is a major faux pas. Even though most of us have one and use it daily, there’s something unappealing about having a big black box against the wall and breaking up the interior flow. It’s become even more of an eyesore now that analog spaces are becoming more popular.

    While one solution is to invest in a TV that can disguise itself as artwork, those come at a high price; the other option is to learn how to hide the TV in a way that doesn’t feel obvious or tacky, and thankfully, designers have a lot of ideas.

    We’ve also included plenty of inspiring photos and expert tips to guide you along the way. If your goal is to reduce the visual presence of technology in your home, you’re in the right place. Keep reading to find inventive ways to make any room feel screen-free—at least when the TV isn’t in use.

    Additional copy by Jessica Cherner.

    Sources indicate that of course, you can hide your television the same way you'd hide anything else you wouldn't want on full display at all times: tuck it into a cabinet. At least, that's what designer Kylie Buhagiar at Melbourne, Australia-based Golden did. "In the main living room, the TV is discreetly integrated into a wall-hung metal joinery box, with hinged doors that elegantly stack back to reveal the screen when needed, maintaining a clean and uncluttered aesthetic," Buhagiar claims. "This thoughtful design transforms the joinery into a sculptural piece of furniture, allowing the space to effortlessly transition from a main living room to a calm sitting area, enhancing the home's rich yet comfortable atmosphere.".

    The whole point of concealing the TV is to hide it, but sometimes, the mechanism used to hide the screen just draws more attention to the area. Gillian Segal, an interior designer based in Vancouver, British Columbia, came up with a clever solution that basically looks like the wall. "This room functioned as both a formal living space and informal family room (complete with movie nights and lots of kids' TV indicates), so we wanted a design that felt both elegant and approachable," Segal explains. "We concealed the TV behind a very simple millwork door system that folds open and closed. It was a cost-effective solution that allowed other elements in the room to shine.".

    It’s no secret that many designers find the Samsung Frame TV to be beautiful, but designer Ariel Okin takes it a step further by adding a literal frame to the Frame. This hidden-TV tactic ensures that it matches other elements in the space, such as the fireplace screen, thus hiding it in plain sight.

    If you don’t want to think about your TV when it’s off, you can cleverly camouflage it. In this living room, designer Emily Del Bello painted a shadowy accent wall black and mounted the TV there—you wouldn't even notice it at first glance.

    In a room as traditional and cohesive as this, you probably don't want a big black rectangle interrupting your aesthetic, so do what designer Lynne Uhalt did and hide your TV in a closet. This guest room is heavily inspired by European interiors and architecture, but Uhalt still wanted the guests to be able to watch TV and relax in bed. As a design-friendly solution, she put the TV in one of the closets, which still boasts enough room to enough to hold clothes.

    Recent findings suggest that designer John Wooden maximized limited square footage in his clients' cottage by cleverly hiding several items, including placing their TV in a beautiful credenza. One of the simplest methods to hide your TV is by incorporating it into furniture that already complements the space. This wooden mid-century piece fits perfectly into the room, making it an ideal spot for a hidden TV.

    In a maximalist, highly colorful space like this, designer Shazalynn Cavin-Winfrey couldn't see how a TV could work in the room, so she decided to hide it in the green cabinet in the back. However, the designer took it a step further and covered the glass with fabric that pulls hues from the rest of the room.

    Industry observers note that everick Brown designed a statement wall encased in custom steel with walnut insets to create a “floating credenza” for a hidden TV. A console table behind the sofa helps separate the two living room zones.

    Recent findings suggest that designed to look like abstract artwork, Kristin Fine hid the TV behind modern paneling above the fireplace. It suits the neutral tones nicely and maintains the refined and grown-up atmosphere while also ensuring that it's family-friendly.

    In a recent development, this living room sitting area revolves around the corner fireplace. To ensure that the TV didn't take up too much valuable visual space, designer Denise McGaha invested in a Samsung Frame and disguised it as a photograph that complements the blue and grey color scheme.

    This outdoor living room, designed by Amanda Lindroth, is the perfect place to entertain and unwind. Look closely at the pagoda-shaped cabinet above the fireplace, and you'll notice that it opens to reveal a hidden TV. It was based on a design from St. Michael's Mount castle in England.

    Recent findings suggest that what do you do in a busy kitchen where the children love TV and the mom doesn't—but she does want to keep an eye on said kids? Enter the Samsung Frame, once again making it all work in family homes with competing interests and preferences, like in April Tomlin Interiors designer Sarah Rogers's kitchen here.

    According to recent reports, A bi-fold panel painting by Stuart Coleman Budd hides a TV, but the goal was to be transparent. “Bronze hinges honestly express that it’s a movable screen—that this is true kinetic art,” says architect Ken Pursley of Pursley Dixon Architecture.

    Recent findings suggest that this formal living room, designed by Mark Cunningham, doubles as a more relaxed and casual hangout room. To ensure that it could do both well, Cunningham built a hidden TV into the back wall shelf that pops up when the occupants want to unwind with a good movie.

    Don’t hide it, just make it one with your wall. This gallery wall of various-sized framed prints blends in with the Samsung Frame TV, which has a wood frame and a rotating display of art images. “None of my clients' guests realize it's a TV when they first walk into the room,” says Natalie Myer of Veneer Designs.

    In a recent development, custom paneling over a fireplace elevates the television area in this bedroom lounge zone by Studio McGee. Flush with the fireplace facade and further disguised by a custom mirror, the hidden TV definitely will not be ruining the chic decor scheme here.

    Related Story: Shea McGee Just Dropped a Cottagecore Home Collab With a Major Fashion Brand.

    Industry observers note that designer CeCe Barfield Thompson hid a TV behind a retractable antique mirror for maximum glamour. “In an oak-paneled Manhattan library, I designed an antique mirror to hide the wall-mounted television,” Thompson says. “The mirror's lower panels retract like a garage door to reveal an entertainment system behind. This mechanism allowed us to create a room that was incredibly functional, without sacrificing an ounce of beauty!”.

    Related Story: This Manhattan Apartment Showcases an Abundance of Antiques and Contemporary Art.

    Here's another example of custom cabinetry with a hidden TV. A sliding door flush with the wood accent wall makes this media room designed by Heidi Caillier extra discreet and pretty. After all, the custom upholstery, drapery, and grasscloth wallpaper are too good to get lost in the entertainment system shuffle.

    According to recent reports, designer Nina Farmer took the most elegant approach possible—hiding the TV in a custom mirrored cabinet atop the mantel. “The living room needed a concealed TV due to the formality of the architecture,” she claims. “Hand-blown mirror was used on the doors so that the enclosure fit with the original 1850s marble mantel. It has concealed hinges and no pull, so when it’s closed, you would never know what’s behind it.”.

    If you can’t outright conceal your screen, the key is to avoid the “black hole” effect when it’s off. “I always try to blend them into the architecture of the house,” says designer Eche Martinez. “We recently completed a project in Belvedere, CA, where the homeowners were hesitant about installing a TV in their living room. To solve this, we decided that the best way to divert attention from the TV when it was not in use was to have an oversized, freestanding piece of art right next to it. Clients loved it, and above all, the piece looks great in the room.".

    #8051. Designers Reveal the Fastest Way They’ve Updated a Living Room Under $100

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (857 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Designers Reveal the Fastest Way They’ve Updated a Living Room Under $100

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A living room is arguably the most popular spot of the house, so why not give it the tender loving care it deserves with a design refresh?
    • According to recent reports, fortunately, affordability and efficiency are no longer mutually exclusive.
    • According to recent reports, barbra Fordyce of Ginger Lemon Indigo says plants are “hands-down” one of the best low-cost, high-impact ways to spruce up your space.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A living room is arguably the most popular spot of the house, so why not give it the tender loving care it deserves with a design refresh? Problem is, when it comes to most home projects, it’s easy to convince yourself good things only come to those who wait—or anyone willing to fork over a small fortune.

    According to recent reports, fortunately, affordability and efficiency are no longer mutually exclusive. According to the pros, it’s possible to elevate a space swiftly and without spending much money. Want proof? Keep scrolling for the clever (and quick) ways designers have upgraded a living room for $100 or less.

    According to recent reports, barbra Fordyce of Ginger Lemon Indigo says plants are “hands-down” one of the best low-cost, high-impact ways to spruce up your space. “Bringing something living into your living room instantly changes the mood, quite literally bringing life, nature and an organic beauty into the room,” explains the designer. While fresh foliage can look good anywhere, she loves how plants can add a “verdant richness” to neutral rooms without throwing off the entire color palette.

    That noted, houseplants aren’t a one-size-fits-all situation, so choose wisely.

    “If you have high ceilings, you want the plant to be proportional to those dimensions,” Fordyce states. “If the plant or tree is too small in a large living room, it will feel dwarfed.”.

    For the perfect finishing touch, use your leftover budget to buy a beautiful planter. “The container should echo the feeling of your room,” she shares. “A basket, ceramic container or even a vintage wooden crate can all make beautiful ‘pots’ for your plants.”.

    Though there is such a thing as too many throw pillows, the right ones can make a difference. “A pillow and throw refresh can go a long way in bringing upcoming life to your sofa,” explains Natalie Kaelin, an interior designer in Raleigh, North Carolina.

    Of course, there’s no need to buy brand-new lumbar and square cushions on a whim: Simply purchase covers for your existing pillows and swap them out seasonally.

    Neutral linen layers can conjure coastal grandmother vibes virtually anywhere, while plush, jewel-toned velvets offer an elegant, autumnal look. Come winter, embrace the holiday spirit with flannel fabric or a plaid repeat.

    We might spend a lot of time talking about layered lighting or how to pick the perfect fixture, but we cannot stress it enough: Pay attention to your bulbs.

    Recent findings suggest that “Daylight LED bulbs are incredibly white, so they put out light akin to doctors’ offices and hospitals,” states Elizabeth Cross-Beard of Palm Henri in Baltimore. “A warmer temperate bulb gives a home a candle-light, cozy feel.” As a general rule of thumb, she recommends buying lightbulbs with a temperature of 2700K and avoiding anything above 4000K.

    Industry observers note that cross-Beard says switching your bulbs can effectively “redesign” your space, and it’s shockingly inexpensive. “Depending on how many lights you have, it can cost as little as $50,” she adds.

    If you want to upgrade your space without spending a cent, Blair Burton notes to start with your furniture.

    “Sometimes simply pulling furniture away from the walls and creating a more comfortable conversation area can completely change how a room feels,” the Austin-based designer explains.

    According to recent reports, after all, just because an armchair has been in the corner of your living room for years doesn’t mean it needs to go there. By doing a room rearrangement, you might end up using it more when it’s in front of a warm, sun-drenched window. Maybe you’ll even realize you need to pick up an ottoman to create the ultimate cozy space.

    Recent findings suggest that another $0 hack? Burton also encourages her clients to “shop their homes.” “It’s practical, of course, but it's also about honoring the things they've collected and loved over the years,” she explains. “Sometimes finding an unexpected latest home for a favorite piece is one of the most satisfying discoveries in a project.”.

    “Adding artwork, whether it's a gallery wall, a single large-scale piece, or something in between, makes a huge visual and personal impact in a living room,” states Molly Torres Portnof of DATE Interiors in Latest York.

    Recent findings suggest that retailers like Minted and Society6 offer well-priced prints, but you can also reframe photographs and posters you already own. As long as you pay attention to scale and proportion, the ceiling’s really the limit. “Rules are meant to be broken,” Portnof states. “If it feels right and makes you happy, you're on the right track.”.

    If your living room is blessed with beautiful built-ins, you can fill them with treasures you already own, or buy a few new pieces for well under $100.

    “Take the time to create vignettes,” advises Tennessee designer Katie Kiser. “More often than not, I find my clients have all the pieces for a well-choreographed space, but they're styled improperly.”.

    For an instant yet affordable upgrade, head over to your local antique store to pick up some art books, jars, or a trinket tray.

    Industry News: Why Your Brand Needs a Gaming Strategy

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1077 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that as our industry counts down to the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, I reflect back to a moment that shaped how I think about gaming.
    • Recent findings suggest that at the time, I was marketing the Pokémon Trading Card Game at Wizards of the Coast, building on my previous gaming experience at GameWorks, before leaving the tabletop business to join the Madden NFL franchise at EA SPORTS, where I eventually became Vice President of Brand Marketing.
    • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI will be a culturally destabilizing event, a game that will reshape the gaming market, where all cultural gravity will be focused on a single product in which all other forms of entertainment will imitate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that as our industry counts down to the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, I reflect back to a moment that shaped how I think about gaming. I was at E3 2001 and was given the opportunity to get hands-on with Grand Theft Auto III. I’d played GTA 2 on PC a couple years earlier, so I understood the franchise, but what I was seeing now was something else entirely. A true, fully realized 3D open world. A city that felt populated, alive, and full of possibility. Characters with personality. And gameplay opportunities around every corner. Rockstar’s vision was unmistakable.

    Recent findings suggest that at the time, I was marketing the Pokémon Trading Card Game at Wizards of the Coast, building on my previous gaming experience at GameWorks, before leaving the tabletop business to join the Madden NFL franchise at EA SPORTS, where I eventually became Vice President of Brand Marketing. My time at EA taught me something fundamental: the connections that brands build between games and their fanbases are powerful. Gamers represent a blue ocean, an enormous, engaged, and largely untapped audience for brands.

    Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI will be a culturally destabilizing event, a game that will reshape the gaming market, where all cultural gravity will be focused on a single product in which all other forms of entertainment will imitate. It is expected to easily outperform the former biggest entertainment launch of all time, Avengers: Endgame, and make more than the combined box office revenue of Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three.

    Recent findings suggest that grand Theft Auto VI is the tip of the spear for console gaming’s resurgence. Industry data partner Circana recently reported physical video game software unit sales up 40% year-over-year, with digital marketplaces setting new concurrent user records almost every month. There are now 150 million new consoles in the market, and more games being released for them than ever before. Gaming has continued to extend its lead as the dominant global entertainment segment.

    According to recent reports, with all of this momentum we’re seeing a ton of brands dipping their toe in the gaming market right now, attempting to recreate the aesthetic of Grand Theft Auto VI, trying to be a part of the conversation. But Grand Theft Auto VI isn’t a fit for brands that are used to risk-adverse advertising campaigns. And truthfully, Rockstar doesn’t need a brand marketing partner. When the entire world is expected to buy your game on day one, there’s nothing a brand could offer that moves the needle. Brands are better off collaborating with gaming properties that are seeking support and fit their cultural ethos, joining those in the gaming space who have already figured this out.

    For those looking to figure out how to authentically market to gamers, there’s already a fair number of successful case studies we’ve been a part of.

    The beauty brand OPI consistently explores ways of engaging with new audiences. Women make up 50% of the video game audience but remain underserved in the market. They worked with Xbox to come up with a colorful partnership: a nail polish line aimed directly at female gamers, which saw immediate sellouts, backed by an experiential campaign in select Target stores. The program’s success led to a second activation the following year that expanded beyond beauty to include the Sunkissed Vibes OPI Special Edition Xbox Controller.

    According to recent reports, IKEA recently tackled a different segment entirely: the physical environment where gaming happens. Both brands’ top designers collaborated on a collection focused on the gamer’s space, solving problems they’re really good at: cord clutter, controller posture, and adaptable living setups. Its popularity demonstrated how a brand can find an original, authentic way to connect with gamers by genuinely improving their experience.

    Fanta found a rare opening in the beverage category that fit their evolving entertainment strategy. They partnered with Xbox as an entry point to bring gamers their delicious Fanta and exclusive in-game rewards. Fanta continued their reputation of going big, and this one included promotional cans being distributed in over sixty countries. Each can was wrapped in exclusive artwork and the collaboration featured an entirely new flavor, Fanta Crimson Sour Cherry. The activation saw over a billion online impressions before a single dollar of media spend was used, a credit to the enthusiasm both fanbases have for their products.

    In a recent development, trolli entered the space after their data revealed that gaming was their audience’s biggest hobby. We helped them build a long-term strategy anchored by exclusive giveaways through unique CPG collaborations and League Trolli, an ongoing esports program that connected them with gamers through competition and prizes. This created an always-on consistency that formed an authentic, reliable relationship with their core demographic.

    It has been revealed that these successful activations within the gaming community require a complete understanding of the gaming experience. Brands succeed when they move beyond superficial advertising and instead deliver tangible value that resonates with gaming audiences, earning organic buzz and fan enthusiasm as a result. Finding an authentic point of connection with gamers through a brand’s existing strengths creates the inflection point of success. Brands should offer genuine value, whether that’s representation, utility, exclusivity, or sustained engagement, in a way that feels true to both the brands and gaming community.

    Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto V shipped in 2013 and has gone on to sell 230 million copies. In the thirteen years since, we’ve watched pioneering brands enter mainstream gaming and find enormous success, while others have yet to figure out their own true path. Brands can’t be a tourist in the gaming space. Don’t let another thirteen years pass before creating a strategy for the biggest entertainment market in the world.

    Recent findings suggest that chris Erb is the head of gaming at CAA Brand Consulting, a division of leading entertainment and sports agency Creative Artists Agency (CAA). Based in Los Angeles, Erb brings expertise across traditional gaming, entertainment, and culture. He oversees potential client opportunities and gaming strategies, working collaboratively across the division to ensure the best teams and expertise are brought forward. Erb has worked with gaming clients, including Microsoft, Bethesda, CD Projekt Red, and Sega, as well as traditional brands, including WK Kellogg’s, Doritos, and Fanta. Prior to CAA Brand Consulting, Erb worked at Electronic Arts, where he led its Madden NFL franchise and EA SPORTS brand.

    Latest Update: Your Houseplants Need a Upcoming Care Routine for Winter—Here Are 4 Easy Habits to Start

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • With colder weather drawing our attention indoors, many of us swap outdoor garden maintenance for caring for our favorite houseplants.
    • Reduced daylight, cooler temperatures, and drier indoor air can all affect the health of houseplants, meaning the care routine that worked perfectly in summer could actually do more harm than good during the colder months.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    With colder weather drawing our attention indoors, many of us swap outdoor garden maintenance for caring for our favorite houseplants. But while your spider plant, peace lily, or monstera may be safely tucked away inside, their needs change significantly during autumn and winter.

    Reduced daylight, cooler temperatures, and drier indoor air can all affect the health of houseplants, meaning the care routine that worked perfectly in summer could actually do more harm than good during the colder months.

    It turns out many of us are unknowingly making a few common mistakes that can leave indoor plants struggling through winter. Here are the habits to avoid, plus the simple swaps that will help keep your houseplants healthy until spring.

    You might assume that moving your houseplant closer to a bright window is an excellent idea in winter to allow it to drink in as much sunlight as possible. And while this isn't necessarily a bad move, it just requires a little more thought.

    It has been revealed that “It’s always a good idea to move them closer to a bright window as darker days hit, but make sure to avoid cold drafts and radiators,” Mark Sage, B&Q's horticulture expert, tells us. “Cold drafts and dry air from radiators can all take their toll on indoor plants, leading to yellowing leaves, rotten roots or even plant fatality.”.

    Similarly, Sage suggests thinking about where the sun actually shines in your home throughout autumn and winter.

    “Where natural light may be limited, consider investing in a plant light to give an extra boost, while rotating larger plants daily can help avoid leggy, awkward growth as they stretch out looking for the sunshine,” he suggests.

    When houseplants start to look a little worse for wear and growth begins to slow over winter, it's tempting to step up your care routine. You might find yourself watering more often, tending to leaves more regularly, or even feeding plants in an attempt to encourage new growth.

    Recent findings suggest that however, Sage warns that this is often the wrong approach. In fact, during autumn and winter, “sometimes the best thing you can do for your plants is leave them alone!”.

    He explains: “In a slower growth period, plants generally need less water and feeding, and winter certainly isn’t the time for regular repotting.”.

    Sources indicate that instead, Sage recommends letting the soil dry out between waterings to help prevent root rot and giving plants time to rest. “It's worth giving them a boost of plant feed ahead of the winter months, but a little goes a long way,” he says. “Give plants their final dose at the end of autumn.”.

    During summer, when houseplants are actively growing, it's common to spread them throughout your home so you can enjoy a touch of greenery in different rooms. However, according to Sage, this can work against them once temperatures drop.

    Instead, he recommends bringing your plants together during autumn and winter to help recreate the conditions many tropical houseplants naturally prefer.

    “Give your houseplants a helping hand through winter by clustering them together to create a more humid microclimate, as many of these plants originally come from much hotter parts of the world,” he recommends. “Grouping several varieties close together can help maintain humidity around them, which can be particularly useful when central heating makes indoor air drier.”.

    While watering may have been your main plant-care task during summer, it's a mistake to neglect cleaning your houseplants over autumn and winter. Just like the rest of your home, plants can gather dust, and that build-up can make it harder for them to make the most of limited daylight.

    Industry observers note that “During winter, leaves can gather a layer of dust,” says Sage. “Give them a wipe down every one to two weeks with a microfibre cloth to support photosynthesis, and to help them benefit from even the smallest burst of sunlight.”.

    In fact, Sage suggests combining cleaning and watering occasionally by giving your plants a gentle shower.

    “Use lukewarm water to boost humidity and get rid of any pests, but keep an eye on the temperature as if it is too cold you can shock the roots, but too warm and you can scald the leaves.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, want to improve your sleep naturally?
    • It has been revealed that plants may also help calm the mind and move the body from an alert state toward a more restful one, potentially supporting better sleep.
    • Recent findings suggest that ahead, find the best plants for your bedroom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, want to improve your sleep naturally? Try adding a few plants to your bedroom. Beyond offering charm and a cozy atmosphere, plants have been linked to mental and physical benefits, including sleep. Research suggests that being around greenery can lift your mood, ease stress, and promote a greater sense of well-being. Bringing a touch of nature into your sleeping space may be a simple way to add those positive qualities to the room.

    It has been revealed that plants may also help calm the mind and move the body from an alert state toward a more restful one, potentially supporting better sleep. A past study linked indoor greenery with more positive emotions and fewer negative ones, which may help you fall asleep faster. The findings point to a broader connection between greenery and well-being, including its possible role in a restful bedroom. It’s easy to see why biophilic design—an approach that evokes nature indoors—has become a favorite among designers.

    Recent findings suggest that ahead, find the best plants for your bedroom. We made sure the options would thrive in all types of lights, but especially in low light, so that whether you’re a beginner or an experienced green thumb, you will find the right verdant friend to grow.

    According to recent reports, the Aspidistra elatior thrives in low to bright shade, making it perfect for bedrooms that don’t get too much direct light. A fun fact: This plant historically was referred to as the “bar room” plant or “beer plant” because it could survive smoky, low-light conditions in Victorian-era taverns and halls. It is non-toxic to humans, cats, and dogs so if you have pets this is a great option.

    Native to the rainforests of Brazil, the Maranta leuconeura is now a common indoor houseplant. During the day, the oval leaves lie flat to soak up the light and at night, the leaves fold upward like praying hands, hence the name.

    It has been revealed that for a trailing plant that thrives in bright, indirect light get a wax plant. It appreciates higher humidity levels so if you live in an older home with fluctuating humidity, this is the verdant plant baby for you.

    For beginner and intermediate plant owners, the nerve plant is a great option because they thrive in most indoor conditions, remain compact, and are safe for pets. They will signal to you what they need so you can water and choose the soil for it accordingly.

    According to recent reports, pilea peperomioides, or the Chinese money plant, is a cheerful-looking, easy-to-propagate plant that is incredibly low-maintenance. It's a great plant for a sunny bedroom. All plant parents need to do is place it in bright, indirect sunlight and water only when the top inch of soil feels dry.

    Aglaonema tolerates very low light levels, so it's ideal if you don't have large windows in your bedroom. Water it when the top few inches of soil feel dry.

    The snake plant doesn't mind low light—and because it's a succulent, it only needs to be watered every week or two.

    Purported to bring good luck, the money tree has a nice, modern vibe—plus, it's not fussy and grows quickly. Give it medium light, water it every week or two, and it'll be happy.

    Sources indicate that the pothos plant tolerates any light level from low to high. (That means it's super-easy to keep alive!) Just don't water it until the top few inches of soil feel dry to the touch—overwatering is the only real way to kill this plant.

    Lavender has long been considered beneficial for relaxation and sleep. Although most research has studied the use of lavender essential oils specifically, having a live lavender plant in your bedroom probably can't hurt. It needs bright light, so make sure it's on a sunny windowsill or use a grow light. Water when the top inch or two feels dry to the touch.

    Sources indicate that this handsome vining plant is a great choice for new plant parents. Its glossy, heart-shaped leaves are beautiful as they spill over the edges of nightstands or bookshelves–and it's tolerant of low light levels. Water when the top few inches of soil feel dry.

    In a recent development, this adorable fern is one of the best to raise indoors. Its thick, waxy leaves retain water better than many other ferns that have finer fronds—and it won't leave a mess by dropping foliage every day. Give it bright indirect light and water when the top inch of soil feels dry.

    In a recent development, this fun plant looks like an old-fashioned ric rac trim. It will grow like crazy in bright indirect light—and because it's a succulent, it needs watering only every week to 10 days.

    This social media darling is striking and easy to grow—it just needs bright indirect light. Water when the top few inches of soil feel dry.

    The peace lily will adapt well to low light levels, but it needs bright indirect light to bloom. Water when the top inch or two feel dry.

    This cute palm that looks just like a messy ponytail likes bright indirect light. And the bulbous base stores water, so it needs a drink only every few weeks when the soil is totally dry.

    This handsome plant boasts a beautiful upright form, so it makes an eye-catching statement in the bedroom. Give it bright indirect light, and water when the top few inches of soil are dry. As an outdoor landscape plant, it will flower, though that's unusual indoors.

    According to recent reports, if you're looking for low-maintenance houseplants, this is the way to go! It will tolerate low light and is often grown in water. In water, change it weekly; in soil, water so that it stays slightly moist.

    This cute tabletop palm will add loads of style to your bedroom. It prefers bright indirect light, but it will tolerate medium light better than many other types of palms. Water when it's slightly dry to the touch.

    #8039. Inside the Houdini Estate—and the Story Behind Its Famous Name

    📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (527 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    Inside the Houdini Estate—and the Story Behind Its Famous Name

    📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, A century after Harry Houdini’s death, the magician’s name still draws visitors to a Los Angeles estate he never owned.
    • The original mansion was destroyed by a fire in 1959, but surviving stone stairways, archways, and a carriage house became part of the property’s later restoration.
    • In a recent development, the estate began as a lavish home for Walker, who built a Mediterranean-style mansion in Laurel Canyon in 1915.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, A century after Harry Houdini’s death, the magician’s name still draws visitors to a Los Angeles estate he never owned. The Houdini Estate, a terraced property in Laurel Canyon now used for events, originally belonged to developer Ralf M. Walker. Its connection to Houdini himself owes much to his wife and stage partner, Bess, who lived across the street after his death and entertained guests in Walker’s gardens.

    The original mansion was destroyed by a fire in 1959, but surviving stone stairways, archways, and a carriage house became part of the property’s later restoration. With the centennial of Houdini’s death falling this Halloween, we’re taking a look back at the history of the Houdini Estate.

    In a recent development, the estate began as a lavish home for Walker, who built a Mediterranean-style mansion in Laurel Canyon in 1915. Its 11 bedrooms and nine bathrooms were joined by a ballroom and a stage. Walker also owned a smaller guesthouse across the street, where Houdini and Bess are mentioned to have briefly stayed while he was filming The Grim Game and Terror Island in 1919.

    Recent findings suggest that bess lived in the guesthouse again with her manager Edward Saint after Houdini’s death in 1926. She also used Walker’s gardens across the street for entertaining, including a 1935 party for hundreds of visiting magicians and their spouses. According to Houdini historian Patrick Culliton, coverage of that gathering helped spread the “Houdini House” name to Walker’s mansion. Over time, the distinction between Bess’s residence and the larger estate blurred.

    Sources indicate that the name persisted long after Bess left. When the mansion burned in 1959, newspapers described it as the “old Houdini mansion,” reinforcing the association even though it had never belonged to him.

    The original mansion and guesthouse were destroyed in the 1959 Laurel Canyon fire. The burned remains of the mansion stood until 1970, when they were demolished. A carriage house survived on the larger property, along with stone stairways, archways, and garden paths.

    In a recent development, owner José Luis Nazar later restored the grounds and developed the property as a venue for events and filming. His work followed decades in which the overgrown ruins had attracted visitors who believed they were exploring Houdini’s former home. The restoration features landscaped terraces, waterfalls, gates, and renewed use of the property’s natural spring.

    The estate now has five acres spread across nine outdoor terraced levels, with trees, sculptures, a koi pond, and waterfalls. The terraces provide separate spaces for meals, ceremonies, and other gatherings, while paths and stairways connect the hillside gardens.

    Recent findings suggest that the current house has four bedrooms, according to the estate’s rental information, while the grounds include a swimming pool and indoor and outdoor spas. Large paintings of Houdini decorate the interiors. The property is privately owned and operated.

    Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, we’re always curious to peek inside celebrities’ homes, whether it’s Kendrick Lamar's Brentwood mansion or Gwyneth Paltrow's Los Angeles estate. With Jay-Z set to headline the 2027 Super Bowl halftime show, we’re turning our attention to the impressive real estate portfolio he shares with Beyoncé (who is no stranger to the halftime stage herself). Over the years, they've spent hundreds of millions on their dream homes, often working with notable architects to find hidden gems on both the east and west coasts.

    The duo have bought and sold several properties in the last decade or so, including a $10 million midtown Manhattan penthouse. But we're most interested in the homes they currently own, and we have all the details. Here, find out where the ultimate power couple spends their days.

    According to recent reports, in 2023, Beyoncé and Jay-Z spent $200 million on a mansion in Malibu, according to TMZ, which went untouched in the recent L.A. fires. The house was designed by renown architect Tadao Ando, whose previous works have been owned by the likes of Kanye West. The 30,000 square-foot compound looks over the Pacific Ocean from the cliffs above, and features Ando's signature concrete-and-glass construction. Photos of the mansion show a museum-like interior, with floor-to-ceiling windows and several pools.

    According to recent reports, in 2017, the power couple spent $88 million on their Bel-Air home, according to Business Insider. Designed by architect Paul McClean, the nearly 19,000-square-foot mansion is yet another modern masterpiece. The home features eight bedrooms, 15 bathrooms, a 15-car garage, and basketball court, alongside outdoor spaces and several pools. One of the key interior features of the house is a spiral staircase that was carved out of a single piece of wood. The annual taxes alone cost nearly $1 million, Realtor.com reported.

    In the ultra-wealthy Tribeca neighborhood of New York, Jay-Z reportedly bought the penthouse apartment in this downtown building in 2004 for $6.8 million. In 2008, this is where the couple got married. The penthouse, located at 195 Hudson Street, reportedly features an elegant balcony. The locale comes with famous neighbors, too: Hailey and Justin Bieber rent in the same building, and Bethenny Frankel is a former resident, according to the Post. A three-bed, 2-bath unit in the building was listed in May, 2024 and sold for $6.6 million, the New York Post reported.

    Beyoncé and Jay-Z reportedly spent $25.9 million on an East Hampton compound aptly named the Pond House, which was originally listed at $35.9 million in 2009. Created by legendary architect Stanford White—who built Madison Square Garden in 1891—the palatial Pond House comes in at 12,000 square feet, and features seven bedrooms and nine bathrooms. The old-school classic elements include parquet floors, marble bathtubs, and 18th-century fireplaces. It was built to overlook the Georgica Pond.

    While it’s never been publicly confirmed, Jay-Z and Beyoncé are the supposed owners of a Spanish Baroque church-turned-residence in the Garden District. An LLC linked to the couple acquired the property in 2015 and put it up for sale in 2021 for $4.45 million, but it never changed hands.

    According to recent reports, geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.
