    #8030. 8 Takeaways from Design Miami and Art Basel in Paris

    📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1023 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    8 Takeaways from Design Miami and Art Basel in Paris

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor.
    • There was plenty of ground to cover in Paris last week where the French editions of Design Miami and Art Basel took place alongside a full slate of noteworthy openings and events.
    • This was the fourth consecutive year that Design Miami, Paris was shown at L’Hôtel de Maisons (the one-time home of Karl Lagerfeld), and the second year that it has been led by Jesse Lee, the proprietor of the luxury resale platform Basic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE Decor editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    There was plenty of ground to cover in Paris last week where the French editions of Design Miami and Art Basel took place alongside a full slate of noteworthy openings and events. (“I have 55 invites this week,” said one harried interiors maven in between stops.) Though the protests in Paris had temporarily subsided by the time the fairs began, they remained top of mind. But still, there was a sense of optimism in the air, which could be chalked up to the unifying power of art and design.

    This was the fourth consecutive year that Design Miami, Paris was shown at L’Hôtel de Maisons (the one-time home of Karl Lagerfeld), and the second year that it has been led by Jesse Lee, the proprietor of the luxury resale platform Basic. Space. Below, a few of the best moments from the week.

    Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn’s Salon 94 Design received the award for Best Gallery Presentation at Design Miami Paris. The Upcoming York gallerist took over the far end of the first floor and filled it with an eclectic mix of pieces: Next to chairs by Alberto Giacometti, she showed furniture—sleek “Stag Stools” replete with protruding antlers—by Rick Owens and Michèle Lamy for the first time. Celebrated artist (and occasional Acne model) Peter Schlesinger quietly stood by as guests admired his large ceramic swan and geese urns, which were fired in a kiln in the garage of his Long Island home. Overlooking it all was a sculptural chandelier by Rome-based designer F. Taylor Colantonio that looked as if it was sliced from the surface of the moon and embedded with gemstones.

    For Apple’s second annual Designers of Tomorrow showcase, a quartet of creators were issued a singular prompt: presence, or rather how to hold people’s attention amid the hurried pace of the modern world. The Brooklyn-based artist Isabel Rower created “Padded Chair, 1860,” which was based on a deep dive into 18th- and 19th-century paper-mâché furniture. Fifteen hundred handmade beads lined the bottom of the piece causing more than one showgoer to comment on the work’s ASMR potential. Other participants included Salem S. Charabi, Yoonjeong Lee, and Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla of Parafernalia. “It was easy to identify these four designers and give them this platform,” said Ago Interiors founder Rodman Primack who served as the curator of the project.

    At Galerie Anne-Sophie Duval in nearby Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the renowned French architect and designer Sylvain Dubuisson presented a series of ogle-worthy pieces: a sleek black desk shellacked with Japanese lacquer, a gold table with metal legs that was designed to oscillate “just for fun,” and another wooden table that was held together vertically by a peg at its center. When the peg was released, the table went horizontal and became a functional dining piece. Another long marble table could be folded into thirds. Even though she no longer runs the gallery (that honor has been bestowed on her daughter, Julie Blum), Duval was on hand on Thursday night to show off Dubuisson’s playful and imaginative inventions.

    The new showroom of ELLE Decor Rising Star Hugo Besnier is an enchanting reminder of all that Paris has to offer. Located in a historic loft off a courtyard in the heart of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the pedigree of previous inhabitants includes Balthus, Sheila Hicks, and even Vanessa Paradis—David Hockney was once a neighbor. In redesigning the property, Besnier took care to include works of these celebrated artists on the walls. The real function of the space is to not only show off his skills as an interior designer, but also his new collection of furniture, Tour de Mains, which works perfectly in the stylized surroundings.

    Shattered prismatic forms by Alteronce Gumby at Jeffrey Deitch and new woven wall hangings by Sheila Hicks at Sikkema Malloy Jenkins were among our favorite pieces that bridged both art and objets. On the Palais’s second level, we encountered Marina Faust’s light sculptures, essentially stripped-down chandeliers hanging from a metal frame. Faust, a former photographer in her seventies, partnered with J. & L. Lobmeyr on these works. They were shown at the booth of Vienna-based gallery Gianni Manhattan.

    At Hauser & Wirth Paris, a very specific collection pinpointed a certain passage in Alexander Calder’s life. Curated by Sandy Rower, the artist’s grandson and the founder and president of the Calder Foundation, Calder: François Premier is an examination of 1953–54 when the artist returned to live in the French countryside and had a very productive year both in terms of creating mobiles—Les Granettes (1953), and The Putney Mobile (1954)—trippy ink and gouache paintings, and household bric-a-brac like a homemade metal tea strainer.

    French filmmaker Alice Diop, in her second collaboration with Miu Miu, presented Geste de Consolation at the Palais d’Iéna where Miu Miu stages its bi-annual runway highlights. The project was the director’s first foray into making an exhibition, and the sampling of works packed a powerful punch. The four interconnected vignettes included a powerful 11-minute video directed by Diop; a purple-hued library and living room space with a curation of Diop’s favorite books and authors such as Chantal Akerman and Christina Sharpe; an ode to an African deity in Simone Leigh’s 16-foot-tall sculpture, Sentinel (Mami Wata); and a poignant photograph by Zanele Muholi. Just beyond the library in the makeshift auditorium, Ivorian choreographer Nadia Beugré arranged for live performances, while concerts were conducted by Angel Bat Dawid and the Sistazz of the Nitty Gritty.

    The week even yielded a surprise appearance by Madonna, who was in town to celebrate her son Rocco Ritchie’s latest exhibition Back on the Brush—a collection of 11 figurative expressionist paintings and sculptures that were shown at Pierre Augustin Rose. On view until November 7, the richly textured works are “rooted in observation, memory, and lived experience.” Says mom: “I love what he is doing!”.

    Sarah Cristobal is a writer, editor, and creative consultant. She is currently editor-at-large for 10 Magazine USA, among other freelance projects.

    #8015. Inside Banqueting House, the Last Surviving Piece of the Lost Palace of Whitehall

    📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    Inside Banqueting House, the Last Surviving Piece of the Lost Palace of Whitehall

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In central London, the 400-year-old Banqueting House is keeping a piece of Britain’s history alive.
    • While Banqueting House indicates how proportion, decoration, and fine art can come together in grandeur, it also stands as a reminder of the Stuart era and how quickly power and glory can fade.
    • According to Historic Royal Palaces, the Palace of Whitehall started out as York Place, which was the London home of the Archbishops of York.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In central London, the 400-year-old Banqueting House is keeping a piece of Britain’s history alive. As the last surviving structure of the former Palace of Whitehall, the landmark highlights royal legacy, classical architecture, and art with its crowning feature: a massive ceiling painted by Flemish Baroque artist Peter Paul Rubens almost four centuries ago.

    While Banqueting House indicates how proportion, decoration, and fine art can come together in grandeur, it also stands as a reminder of the Stuart era and how quickly power and glory can fade.

    According to Historic Royal Palaces, the Palace of Whitehall started out as York Place, which was the London home of the Archbishops of York. When Cardinal Thomas Wolsey lost power, Henry VIII took over the property and turned it into a royal palace, calling it Whitehall. It became a primary location for Tudor and Stuart court life, where royal ceremonies, political drama, and entertainment took place.

    Recent findings suggest that the building that stands today was completed in 1622 for James I, who wanted a grand setting for court celebrations. It was the third banqueting house built on the site, replacing an earlier structure whose columns blocked people’s views of the festivities.

    A 1698 fire destroyed most of the complex, leaving Banqueting House as its sole remnant.

    In a recent development, architect Inigo Jones brought Palladian ideas, which center around classical symmetry and proportion, into English royal architecture. He traveled in France and Italy to study ancient Roman and Renaissance buildings, then used what he learned at Whitehall.

    The exterior originally combined honey-hued and pinkish-brown stone with decorative details in white Portland stone. It took two phases of work to give the facade its more current, uniform pale appearance: partial refacing in 1774, followed by a larger restoration starting in 1829, led by architect John Soane.

    Industry observers note that inside, the main hall is a so-called “double cube,” meaning it’s twice as long as it is wide and tall. These proportions make the space feel open and balanced, encouraging visitors to look up.

    Jones designed the hall for masques—elaborate indicates with music, dance, poetry, and costumes—which honored the monarch and supported Stuart rule. Under the main hall, a vaulted undercroft served as a drinking den for James I and his friends.

    The most famous part of Banqueting House is its nine-panel ceiling, painted by Rubens. Conversations about the paintings started under King James I’s rule, but his son Charles I officially ordered them in 1629 to honor his father as well as the Stuart family. Rubens finished the paintings in Antwerp in 1634, and they were installed two years later. The artist made £3,000 and recieved a gold chain for his work.

    Together, the works cover more than 2,400 square feet. The three main paintings depict James I joining the English and Scottish crowns, ruling with wisdom, and rising toward the heavens. The other scenes use classical myths to support the idea that the Stuart monarchy was chosen by divine right.

    It has been revealed that jones designed the ceiling to accommodate the giant canvases, setting them into a frame of carved and gilded wood. The classical architectural details help balance Rubens’s dramatic figures and movement.

    Banqueting House is also linked to the fall of the very monarchy it was meant to celebrate. On January 30, 1649, Charles I walked through the building and out to a scaffold set up outside, where he was executed after the English Civil War. Less than 15 years after Rubens’s paintings were put up, the king passed under the ceiling he had commissioned in honor of his father as he went to his death.

    Sources indicate that the building later saw the return of the monarchy and was used for other royal events, including an old healing ritual called the “King’s Evil,” where monarchs touched people thought to have a skin disease, hoping to cure them. The hall was also used to give out Maundy money to the poor before Easter.

    Brea Cubit is an award-winning journalist who covers culture, entertainment, fashion, business, and more. When she’s not writing and editing, she enjoys listening to live music, binge-watching nostalgic TV, and shopping at artisan markets.

    #8011. 14 Everyday Home Items You Need to Replace More Often Than You Think

    📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1510 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    14 Everyday Home Items You Need to Replace More Often Than You Think

    📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • Recent findings suggest that your home might be a showcase of timeless design, with stylish accessories, custom artwork, and high-end furniture.
    • According to recent reports, “Even the most gorgeous spaces lose their charm if we forget to patch essentials,” states Linda Hayslett, principal designer at LH.Designs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    Recent findings suggest that your home might be a showcase of timeless design, with stylish accessories, custom artwork, and high-end furniture. But when the everyday things that keep a household functioning are left unattended to for long enough, the space may be less clean and organized (and safe!) than it looks.

    According to recent reports, “Even the most gorgeous spaces lose their charm if we forget to patch essentials,” states Linda Hayslett, principal designer at LH.Designs. “Keeping your home looking and feeling fresh isn’t just about design—it’s also about the little things.”.

    It has been revealed that caring for your home means looking beyond the interiors. Giving neglected areas the attention they need can keep germs and grime at bay, and replacing certain items can also protect your health and safety. Consider your carbon monoxide alarm: If an aging unit fails during an emergency, the consequences could be deadly.

    Recent findings suggest that to help you keep everything in good shape, we asked experts which 14 household items you should replace as soon as possible. Take a look—you can thank us later!

    When to replace: five to 10 years.

    Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors lose their sensitivity over time, which could delay detection during an emergency. The timeframe for when you should replace these will vary by manufacturer. Look up the model you have online to be sure—even a fairly latest alarm should be tested once a month. The batteries should be replaced once a year.

    When to replace: six months to one year.

    Industry observers note that mold and mildew can build up on shower liners, especially in damp environments. A 2024 study by SafeHome.org revealed that shower curtains had the most germs of any other surfaces in the bathroom, including the toilet seat. While Hayslett recommends washing them every three months, the material can eventually become brittle over time.

    When to replace: one to three years.

    It has been revealed that dingy towels are the antithesis of luxe. Towels lose their absorbency and softness after years of washing.

    “Avoid using too much detergent, which can build up on fibers,” Hayslett says. “Use a little vinegar during the rinse cycle to keep towels soft.” If your bath towels feel scratchy or start to smell musty despite washing, it’s time for a refresh.

    To prolong the life of your towels, make sure you let them dry properly between uses to prevent mildew growth, noted Vyanca Soto of Market Studio Interiors. And you should definitely swap them out if you notice discoloration from your skincare products.

    You likely spend plenty of time in your kitchen and bathroom each day. Make sure you take a few minutes to examine the grout lines around your bathtub and kitchen countertops.

    “Grout breaks down over time, and you can end up with water damage to the drywall,” indicates Rebekah Zaveloff, cofounder and creative director at Imparfait Design Studio. “If you look and there are spots that have pulled away or deteriorated, it’s time to regrout.”.

    When to replace: seven to 10 years.

    A sagging mattress is a clear sign it’s time for a upcoming one. Mattresses lose support and can accumulate dust mites, allergens, and even mold, which is certainly not a dreamy way to slumber.

    “Flip your mattress every six months [unless it's a one-sided design] to help maintain its structure and extend its lifespan,” Hayslette advised.

    According to recent reports, A mattress protector can extend its lifespan as does regular vacuuming to remove dust and debris. Soto recently bought a bed vacuum cleaner and says, “It works like a charm.” She also uses it on her dog’s bed to help it stay clean and smell fresher.

    When to replace: one to two years.

    Industry observers note that the lifespan of a pillow mainly depends on its material, whether that be foam, feathers, or another type of synthetic fill. But once a pillow of any kind loses its shape, it's time to say goodbye. Like mattresses, pillows can harbor dust mites, dead skin cells, and sweat over time. You can prolong a pillow's life with a pillow protector—Soto likes the Serta Power Chill—but you should still swap those out every year or so.

    When to replace: two to three years for sheets; five to 10 years for duvets.

    Bed linen care and personal hygiene dictate the condition of your linens. Similar to pillows, sheets and duvets can accumulate dust mites, allergens, and bacteria, especially if you allow kids or pets into your bed.

    “Over time, duvets lose their fluffiness and insulating properties due to regular use and washing,” says Rebecca Bobroff of Rebecca Bobroff Design.

    If you’re prone to night sweats or use a lot of skin-care products, you may notice that your sheets become quickly discolored. Along with regular washing, you may want to stick to white sheets you can bleach over colors, which will look dingy even when they're clean.

    Recent findings suggest that “At a minimum, wash pillowcases once a week,” says Danielle Hurhula, head of home merchandising for Quince. “I’d recommend bumping washes up to twice a week if you suffer from allergies or asthma, sleep with hair or skincare products, or have sensitive or acne-prone skin.”.

    When to replace: three to six months.

    HVAC maintenance experts, including Energy Star, recommend checking filters monthly and replacing air filters every three months to help your system function properly and keep dust and allergens out of your home.

    If you remove your filters and they look extra dirty, you may want to up the frequency. Doing so will not only improve indoor quality but keep your HVAC system from overworking and wasting energy, which could shave a few years off its life.

    When to replace: six months to one year.

    Water filters can accumulate bacteria, minerals, and other contaminants. This can affect the taste and quality of your drinking water.

    “The lifespan of a filter cartridge is influenced by the level of contaminants and particulates in your water,” notes Eric Roy, Ph.D., founder and chief scientist at Hydroviv. “Sink filter cartridges should be replaced approximately every six months and are designed to handle up to 720 gallons of water.”.

    You should also watch for a decrease in the flow rate, which indicates the filter is saturated.

    When to replace: five years (or as recommended by the manufacturer).

    You likely know that fridge water filters should be replaced every six months, but water lines can build up gunk or start leaking over time.

    “Inspect the line for cracks or discoloration every year,” Soto suggests. “Flush it with vinegar and water every six months to prevent mineral buildup and ensure clean, clear water. My mom taught me this and when you see the color of the water when you flush it—you'll never stop doing it.”.

    When to replace: one to five years.

    Using sharp knives on wooden and plastic cutting boards can create grooves that embed bacteria, even after a dishwasher cycle. One study revealed that plastic surfaces have the longest bacteria survival time, and scraping wooden boards with a knife significantly reduced bacterial presence.

    According to recent reports, soto disinfects cutting boards with a vinegar solution and uses bleach for plastic boards. “Sand down wooden boards occasionally to remove deep grooves and re-oil them to maintain the wood,” she says.

    When to replace: one to two weeks.

    Recent findings suggest that sponges harbor bacteria, especially when you use them to clean up raw food such as eggs and meat. In fact, salmonella can thrive on a sponge for more than seven days. Hayslette’s tip: Microwave damp sponges for one minute to sanitize between uses, but toss them after two weeks max.

    Recent findings suggest that keep sponges as dry as possible, or better yet, replace them with dish brushes as these are less likely to breed bacteria, according to the International Journal of Food Microbiology. We like the Curio dish brush because it stands upright on a magnetic pedestal and you can replace the brush heads.

    When to replace: three to five years (or sooner if scratched).

    It has been revealed that the nonstick coating on your cookware can wear off or become damaged over time. This decreases a pan's efficacy and also makes it a health hazard—the coating may start to flake off into your food.

    “To extend their life, always use nonmetal utensils and hand-wash your pans instead of placing them in the dishwasher,” Hayslette states.

    When to replace: two to three years.

    Not only do latex anti-slip rug pads lose cushioning over time, but they can also start to disintegrate.

    Sources indicate that “They get tacky and sticky on the floor, which can damage the floor's surface,” Zaveloff explains. Pull up your rug once in a while and if you see that the rug pads are turning dark yellow, start shopping for upcoming ones.

    Does Your Home Need a Porte-Cochère? Architects Explain When the Statement Feature Works Best

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Few architectural features make a statement like a porte-cochère.
    • The term porte-cochère translates from French as “coach door.” The feature has a highbrow history: horse-drawn carriages once pulled up beneath porte-cochères at King Louis XIV’s château.
    • It has been revealed that “The easy answer as to why we love porte-cocherès is the weather,” notes Utah-based designer Kristina Lawrence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Few architectural features make a statement like a porte-cochère. A covered entrance gives a home a certain panache, but your house doesn’t have to look like something out of HBO’s The Gilded Age to pull it off.

    The term porte-cochère translates from French as “coach door.” The feature has a highbrow history: horse-drawn carriages once pulled up beneath porte-cochères at King Louis XIV’s château. But it works just as well in the modern era.

    It has been revealed that “The easy answer as to why we love porte-cocherès is the weather,” notes Utah-based designer Kristina Lawrence. “Here in the Park City mountains, a porte-cocherè gives guests a covered place to step out of the car, whether it’s snowing in January or raining in June. And when clients are entertaining, that’s something everyone appreciates.” But how do you know if this structure can actually work on your property?

    According to recent reports, “Because porte-cochères are relatively large structures, typically ranging from 18 by 22 feet to 25 by 30 feet, their scale and relationship to the main house are critical,” says Seth Ballard of Ballard + Mensua Architecture. “Without careful three-dimensional design studies, a porte-cochère can easily appear out of proportion or overwhelm the architecture.”.

    The last thing you want to do is rely on the size of your SUV as a guidepost. Mark Caulfield, director of Glass House Architecture, notes that this type of addition works best with Georgian, Regency, Victorian or large contemporary homes with strong horizontal lines. “The eaves should match to the roofline, and the columns should be slightly above the structural minimum to have the proper visual weight,” Caulfield explains.

    Ahead, here’s when experts say adding a porte-cochère makes sense to your property.

    A porte-cochère is one way to further enhance an already large home.

    According to recent reports, “Extending a roofline away from the house can help balance a tall entry and gives a spacious driveway a more balanced sense of scale and purpose,” Lawrence claims of the above home. “It also creates an incredible feeling of arriving somewhere special.” Not to mention, it’s also incredibly convenient when you pull up to the house with a trunk full of luggage or ski gear, for instance.

    “Add a fireplace nearby for warmth, and it’s like the welcome starts before anyone even walks through the front door,” she adds.

    With the right architectural detail, perhaps an arch, passing through a porte-cochère reveals an entirely different point of view, whether it’s the focus on the home or the landscape view beyond.

    “That unfolding arrival can be one of the most memorable parts of the home,” Lawrence says of another one of her projects above.

    You don’t have to live in a manse to add a porte-cochère. Adding one at the entry to the kitchen or mudroom creates a functional arrival point.

    Industry observers note that “Years of neglect had erased this 1890 home’s Victorian character,” says Dan D’Agostino, founder of Strategy Architecture, of the above project. “So, the clients drew on the Craftsman bungalow they grew up in to guide its latest details.”.

    Here, D'Agostino took advantage of the natural slope to create a porte-cochère that actually works as a bridge carport to link the main house to a guest suite.

    Sources indicate that “It works as the home’s gateway,” he explains. This feature works in any climate, whether you’re escaping from rain or want to provide shade for your car during a heat wave.

    Bob Zuber, a partner with Morgante Wilson Architects, created a porte-cochère that seamlessly blended into the overall architecture of the house. Creating an unobtrusive entryway facade makes this opening more like a doorway than a passage. Adding distinctive lighting and landscaping further enhances the look.

    #7999. Designers Say This High-Gloss Paint Trick Can Make Your Kitchen Look Instantly More Expensive

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (774 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Designers Say This High-Gloss Paint Trick Can Make Your Kitchen Look Instantly More Expensive

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pictured above: This Upcoming York City kitchen by designer Francis Nicdao features a high-gloss-painted island.
    • Once you’ve pinpointed the ideal color palette for your kitchen, you might think that the work is done.
    • Industry observers note that “There is a richness to high-gloss paint that really can't be achieved with any other finish or product, especially in deeper colors,” says Malorie Goldberg, a principal designer at Noa Blake Design.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pictured above: This Upcoming York City kitchen by designer Francis Nicdao features a high-gloss-painted island.

    Once you’ve pinpointed the ideal color palette for your kitchen, you might think that the work is done. But not so fast. The success of your shades really comes down to finish, and there’s real potential in choosing a high-gloss paint. After all, if your kitchen is the showpiece of your home, you should make it shimmer.

    Industry observers note that “There is a richness to high-gloss paint that really can't be achieved with any other finish or product, especially in deeper colors,” says Malorie Goldberg, a principal designer at Noa Blake Design. “A high-gloss finish adds interest to cabinets that makes them feel more like furniture, immediately elevating the overall feel of the space.”.

    This option might be tough to imagine, given that kitchens are typically painted in a matte or eggshell finish. But that doesn’t mean that a shinier upgrade is out of the question. “High-gloss kitchens can be in a small or large space. For a smaller space, a butler's pantry might be a great place to play,” notes Danielle Davis, founder and principal designer of 56th Street Design Studio. “A larger kitchen will likely have a lot of millwork, so high-gloss paint can be applied to surfaces where it can really shine.”.

    In a recent development, if you want to make a statement in your kitchen using the budget-friendly quality of paint, a high-gloss finish could be the right move. Here’s how the pros recommend pulling it off.

    Recent findings suggest that when you’re considering a high-gloss finish, think of how it can be used to complement the rest of your kitchen. If you’re leaning toward trending darker palettes—like chocolate browns, emerald greens, and deep plums—then a high gloss will help bounce light around the room and make undertones more noticeable throughout the day. But if you’re doing just fine with a neutral backdrop, then a high-gloss will only make that look brighter. Either way, “high gloss” is paint speak for highlighter.

    “The way that light reflects off a high-gloss finish adds a brightness that can make the space feel more expansive, even in moodier tones,” says Ariel Fischer, who is also a principal at Noa Blake Design.

    Sources indicate that fischer and Goldberg would likely pick a darker shade on kitchen cabinetry for this effect, which Goldberg notes works on ultramodern panels and more ornate fronts. But Jen Levy, interior designer at Surrounded by Color, says it’s OK to go lighter—while looking up. “I love a high gloss ceiling in a kitchen,” Levy says. “My team and I see it used either way, but my preference is to have this paint treatment punctuate a lighter, brighter space.”.

    Recent findings suggest that paint is often regarded as DIY-friendly, but choosing this finish probably shouldn’t involve you rolling up your sleeves. “Hire a professional,” Levy notes. “High gloss involves a lot of prep work to look right.” Since the results should almost resemble a mirror, Davis echoes this advice. “If a surface isn't perfectly sanded or smooth, high-gloss will show those imperfections,” she says. “It will ultimately take away from that perfect finish you’re after.”.

    In a recent development, as far as the best location for high-gloss paint, Davis has one strong preference. “High-gloss cabinets, from a practical standpoint, are forgiving in terms of wear,” she notes. “You can easily wipe fingerprints, spills, and food right off the cabinet with a microfiber cloth.” Keep in mind, though, that chips will be noticeable, so this probably isn’t the right finish for busy households with young children.

    As you determine the remaining details of your kitchen with a high-gloss paint in mind, remember to keep it front and center. Everything else in this space has to complement that sheen in order for the effect to be successful. “In a rustic kitchen, or one where natural wood is prevalent, high-gloss paint may clash with the overall vibe,” Davis notes. The opposite is also true: A modern kitchen with too many shiny surfaces will feel like a carnival fun house.

    Recent findings suggest that to pull your kitchen together, seek out countertops and flooring with a matte finish alongside lighting and hardware that has a slight sheen. The goal is to find ways to ground the room, even as you center its high-gloss boldness. “I would love to have a client who’s daring enough to do a high-gloss kitchen,” Davis says. “Nevertheless, high-gloss paint can still have a timeless quality, while still having a big impact on the room.”.

    The Blue Door House from Notting Hill Just Hit the Market

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that it’s perhaps the most famous house in one of London’s most charming neighborhoods, so beloved that crowds are known to gather around it like the English version of Carrie Bradshaw’s West Village apartment.
    • Recent findings suggest that despite starring in a blockbuster rom-com, the 2,750-square-foot house in question is very much real—and now it can be yours.
    • Not coincidentally, the three-bedroom residence also once belonged to Richard Curtis, the screenwriter behind Notting Hill, which was directed by Roger Michell and went on to gross some $364 million worldwide.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that it’s perhaps the most famous house in one of London’s most charming neighborhoods, so beloved that crowds are known to gather around it like the English version of Carrie Bradshaw’s West Village apartment. It’s the blue-doored townhouse where Hugh Grant’s fictional bookseller lived and wooed Julia Roberts’s paparazzi-plagued Hollywood actress in 1999’s Notting Hill.

    Recent findings suggest that despite starring in a blockbuster rom-com, the 2,750-square-foot house in question is very much real—and now it can be yours. That is, for roughly $10 million.

    Not coincidentally, the three-bedroom residence also once belonged to Richard Curtis, the screenwriter behind Notting Hill, which was directed by Roger Michell and went on to gross some $364 million worldwide.

    Industry observers note that behind the recognizable front door—painted a glossy, rich shade of royal blue—the house unfolds with an entrance vestibule and courtyard before reaching a cavernous great room topped by a vaulted ceiling and a row of skylights. Nearly 50 feet in length, the soaring space was originally an artist’s studio and now does triple duty as a kitchen, dining, and reception area. The room has hardwood floors, a stone fireplace, deep-green cabinetry, and a marble-topped island. Two guest rooms can also be found elsewhere on the floor, each with its own private bath.

    Upstairs, the primary suite comes with a dual-sink bathroom equipped with both a freestanding tub and a shower. This floor also features a lofted library and office that overlooks the ground level’s central room, plus a spiral staircase that leads to the roof terrace.

    Other outdoor spaces include a small balcony off the second floor and an expansive ground-level courtyard. It might not come with a bumbling Hugh Grant, but the house certainly has charm to spare.

    The Blue Door House is listed for £7.5 million with Josh Ratcliff of UK Sotheby’s International Realty.

    #7990. These 8 Common Heating Mistakes Could Be Costing You More Than You Realize, Experts Warn

    📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1159 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    These 8 Common Heating Mistakes Could Be Costing You More Than You Realize, Experts Warn

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • It has been revealed that staying cozy is a top priority in winter—whether you're curling up on the sofa or getting snug under the covers.
    • From setting the thermostat too high to neglecting to bleed radiators, small heating mistakes can affect how warm your home feels and how much energy you use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    It has been revealed that staying cozy is a top priority in winter—whether you're curling up on the sofa or getting snug under the covers. But turning up the heating isn’t always the answer: some everyday habits can leave your home colder while pushing your bills higher.

    From setting the thermostat too high to neglecting to bleed radiators, small heating mistakes can affect how warm your home feels and how much energy you use.

    To help you stay comfortable without wasting energy, we asked heating experts to share the most common mistakes—and the simple fixes that can make your home warmer and your bills easier to manage.

    It has been revealed that when the chill sets in, it’s tempting to whack the thermostat up a few notches for a quick blast of warmth. But this common habit does more harm than good. “While it won’t heat your home any faster, what it will do is waste energy and therefore waste money,” say the heating specialist experts at Heatforce. “Each degree above 66 degrees Fahrenheit can add a whopping 10 percent to your annual heating costs.”.

    It has been revealed that the smarter approach is to keep your thermostat at around 66 degrees when you’re at home and awake, then drop it by four to six degrees overnight. That way, you’ll stay comfortable without sending your bills soaring.

    When arranging furniture, it’s easy to prioritize style over function—but placing bulky pieces too close to your radiator can drastically reduce its efficiency.

    Industry observers note that “Make sure that furniture and curtains aren’t obstructing this area of your home, as heat needs to be able to circulate freely,” says Amthal Karim, head of design at Furniture & Choice. “Where space allows, move sofas, armchairs, and other large pieces of furniture away from radiators to help warm air circulate more effectively around the room.”.

    According to recent reports, scott Byrom, a home energy expert at The Energy Shop, adds: “A large piece of furniture placed against a radiator can absorb a significant amount of the heat it emits, meaning you're paying to warm the back of your sofa rather than the room. Pulling furniture just six inches away allows warm air to rise and move freely, and you'll feel the difference almost immediately.”.

    Warm air can escape through gaps around doors, windows, and letterboxes, leaving rooms colder and forcing your heating to work harder—which can push up your bills over winter.

    It has been revealed that “Many older homes with hardwood front doors will experience worse drafts in the winter as they are susceptible to expanding in heat and contracting in the cold, meaning gaps around the frame will become even wider,” warns Oliver Novakovic, head of innovation at David Wilson Homes. “To combat this, invest in a draft exclusion runner to go along the bottom of your door. You can also purchase lengths of gap sealer to run around the frame, preventing cold air from blowing in around the door frame.”.

    Draft blockers, letterbox brushes, and simple sealant strips are all inexpensive fixes that can help a home retain heat far more effectively.

    Sources indicate that if you’re relying on an old heated blanket to stay warm, check its age and condition. It may no longer heat as effectively, leaving you tempted to turn up the thermostat and spend more on heating.

    According to recent reports, “Older electric blankets or those without overheating protection can pose a fire hazard,” states Adele Brennan, home electrical buyer at Vonhaus. “However, there are newer, innovative electric blankets that come equipped with an automatic shut-off function.”.

    A newer blanket with an automatic shut-off function is a safer choice, but using one to compensate for a cold room won’t fix the underlying heating problem.

    Recent findings suggest that it might feel indulgent to keep the heating running from dawn until dusk, but it’s an expensive habit that can rapidly inflate your energy bills. “Instead, schedule your heating for convenient times,” states Stephen Hankinson, heating expert at Electric Radiators Direct.

    “For example, if you like being comfortable as you get ready in the morning, program your heating to switch on just before you wake up and then off again by the time you leave.”.

    Sources indicate that this way, you’ll enjoy warmth exactly when you need it, without wasting energy. Just don’t forget to adjust your schedule when the clocks change.

    It has been revealed that it's easy to focus on simply switching radiators on and off, but regular maintenance is just as crucial. Bleeding your radiators is essential for keeping them running efficiently. “After a while, pockets of air can get trapped within the radiators, causing cold spots and preventing hot water from flowing through,” explains Hankinson. “The usual sign your radiator needs bleeding is that the top section is much cooler than the bottom.”.

    To fix this, switch off your heating system, use a radiator key to open the valve, and keep a towel handy to catch any drips of water. Doing this at least once a year will keep your heating even and effective.

    Industry observers note that drying clothes on radiators is common in colder, wetter months, but it can stop heat from circulating around the room. Your heating may then need to stay on longer to reach a comfortable temperature, using more energy and pushing up your bills. A clothes dryer in a well-ventilated room is a better option.

    It has been revealed that “The bigger complications are its contribution to mold and dampness within your home, as well as the inability to heat your home, so you're left with a damp, cold house throughout winter, which is costing you,” states Andy Simms from MyBuilder.com. “Instead, using a clothes drying rail or taking advantage of brighter, milder days to hang your washing outside or open windows can make a real difference. And when drying clothes indoors, using a dehumidifier is effective in keeping moisture low.”.

    It might feel inconvenient to book in a boiler service—especially if it means rearranging your day to be at home—but skipping it can be a costly mistake, as minor complications could go unnoticed, which could reduce its efficiency.

    For peace of mind, it’s best to get your service done in autumn. That way, any small problems are caught early, and you’ll avoid the risk of being left without reliable heating during the coldest months of the year.

    “Having your boiler serviced annually is a great action to take to prevent boiler breakdowns, as well as improve its efficiency. It helps keep your boiler operating at maximum efficiency, consuming less fuel to generate the same amount of heat,” notes Ian Palmer-Smith, appliance repair expert at Domestic & General.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, new York’s Oheka Castle measures nearly 113,000 square feet, making it the nation’s second-largest residence, just behind the historic Biltmore in Asheville, North Carolina. Set on 23 manicured acres atop Long Island’s highest point in Huntington, the massive Jazz Age estate is famous for appearing in a litany of photo shoots, movies, and music videos—such as Orson Welles’s Citizen Kane and Taylor Swift’s “Blank Space.”.

    Industry observers note that built in 1919 by architecture firm Delano & Aldrich with landscaping by the Olmsted Brothers, Oheka is also a popular event space and wedding venue, with a hotel, ballroom, and restaurant on site. But in August 2025, the owner of the 127-room French Renaissance château abruptly filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in a bid to save it from foreclosure. In his filing, owner Gary Melius revealed the property had less than $60 in its checking account and owed creditors some $63.5 million.

    The landmark estate hit the auction block on October 27 with Concierge Auctions, in collaboration with Adam D. Modlin of The Modlin Group. In the bankruptcy proceedings, an appraiser pegged the complex’s value at $137 million. It ultimately fetched $72 million, plus a buyer’s premium.

    According to recent reports, the latest owners are Ronald Browning and Paul Alflen, Gold Coast Property & Estate Management partners, per The New York Post. The auction featured seven bidders competing for the residence out of 740 that had expressed interest during the lead-up. The live auction took place at The Dominick hotel in New York City.

    Before parting with the estate, Melius secured approval to construct 95 luxury condos on the property. Browning and Alflen will retain that authorization as winning bidders.

    In a recent development, regardless of whether those units get built, the landmark estate will be preserved. “We’re going to leave the castle as it is and make sure it keeps its historical presence,” Alflen told Long Island Business News. “We’re excited for what’s coming next.”.

    Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design.     It has been revealed that miele crafts appliances for enduring performance, but they also curate experiences that engage all the senses. Imagine the intuitive precision of a sleek induction cooktop that subtly adjusts temperature on its own; the soft, inviting glow of a French door refrigerator that reveals a curated bounty within ample space; the alluring aroma of a built-in coffee system greeting you each morning; and the calming, almost meditative hum of a steam at work. Each of these choreographed moments elevate Miele appliances beyond a functional tool into something you fundamentally feel. By blending groundbreaking innovation and sustainable features with timeless, minimalist design, Miele frees you to embrace the pure joy of cooking and to savor the intimate, everyday moments that make a house a true home.

    For this year’s Art Basel, the ultimate intersection of culture and creativity, Miele brings together two visionaries to redefine the culinary space. Tiffany Howell of Night Palm Design is passionate about creating cinematic homes that tell a deeply personal story. Asher Young is a multidisciplinary artist known for merging art with technology to create immersive spectacle. Together, they have imagined a sensory kitchen built entirely within a lush botanical garden setting. Here, the wildness of the natural world frames the precise German engineering. It is a space where the smooth, handleless silhouettes and cool touch of Miele's Obsidian Black glass stand in striking relief against their organic surroundings, harnessing technology for a design that is both tactile and state-of-the-art. “We used the sleek, matte black Miele appliances as the driving force to bring this to life,” says Howell of the striking visual contrast between nature and cutting-edge machines. “They’re like the perfect little black dress—timeless, elegant, and grounding the entire room.” A deep respect for the environment is also reflected in Miele engineering, which uses innovative technology that preserves ingredients longer—ensuring that the natural world isn't just an aesthetic inspiration, but a core priority for the brand.

    According to recent reports, howell’s signature nostalgic romance blends with Asher’s analytical thinking and knack for creating physical, interactive experiences to make the space come alive. Young's touch ensures the installation feels genuinely dynamic, translating the unseen power of Miele’s technology into a captivating physical experience. “How can we create a space that rebalances and also is a place that you can actually engage with? So you can smell the flowers while you're washing your hand. You can feel the cool breeze as you open the fridge,” explains Young. “All these elements is not just for the sake of a visual presentation, but actually to experience and be inside.” The result is an experiential reminder that kitchens should always reflect your personality and passions. “We both mentioned let’s bring our shared language together,” he recalls. The finished design is the undeniable heartbeat of the garden, a space with one foot rooted elegantly in the past and the other stepping boldly into the future.

    “A kitchen expresses how you live, what you love and desire, and it’s also where your most cherished memories are made,” notes Howell. As the Miami sun sets, the botanical space seamlessly transitions into an elegant, moody enclave for evening entertaining, inviting you to linger just a little bit longer. And in a Miele kitchen, those memories continue into the next day, beginning the moment the fragrant aroma of freshly brewed coffee introduces the limitless possibilities of a brand-latest morning.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A year after Titanic won a record 11 Academy Awards and made history as the highest grossing movie of all time, Céline Dion—who sang the 1997 film’s most memorable song, “My Heart Will Go On”—completed a custom mansion in Jupiter, Florida, a few miles north of Palm Beach. The French-Canadian Grammy winner lived there for four years, selling the Mediterranean-style mansion in 2002 for $9 million, per Zillow.

    In a recent development, now, the palatial retreat just traded hands again in an off-market deal to investor Myron Miller, who paid $12 million for the 14,700-square-foot retreat. The seller’s agent was Rob Thomson of Waterfront Properties, while Miller was represented by Willie Abreu of The Nicolas Group at SERHANT.

    Although the transaction was made privately, the eight-bedroom, 11-bath estate had originally been listed for $20 million in May, only to be taken off the market in August. The sale closed October 23, per Zillow.

    It has been revealed that set behind gates in Admirals Cove, the two-story waterfront residence features checkerboard flooring, coffered ceilings, elaborate moldings, and gilded fixtures. Among the perks are a home cinema, a wood-paneled office, a fountain, and plenty of areas for entertaining. The area is known to attract celebrity residents like Michael Jordan, Tiger Woods, and Wayne Gretzky.

    The .65-acre grounds come with manicured gardens, a pool, a gazebo, and a dock on Lake Worth Creek, which connects to the Atlantic Ocean.

    Sources indicate that after selling the property, Dion later built another custom home in the South Florida community—this one inspired by the architecture of the Bahamas and equipped with a water park. She ultimately sold that property for $28 million.

    According to recent reports, dion, who disclosed she was battling stiff-person syndrome in 2023, recently wrapped the first leg of her new residency, Celine Dion Paris, hauling in $125.5 million from 539,000 tickets sold, according to Billboard. Ten additional highlights are slated for next year.

    How Often Should You Be Cleaning Your Leather Furniture? It's More Often Than You Think

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • Pictured above: A leather seat in a space designed by Jill Tran of Tran + Thomas Design Studio.
    • In a recent development, no one invests in a piece of leather furniture with prepares to replace it again in just a few years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    Pictured above: A leather seat in a space designed by Jill Tran of Tran + Thomas Design Studio.

    In a recent development, no one invests in a piece of leather furniture with prepares to replace it again in just a few years. After all, a full-grain leather sofa can go decades without cracking, and minor scuffs simply add to the patina.

    But the key lies in how well you care for your leather furniture. Leather may be lower maintenance than fabric upholstery, but it still needs occasional TLC to last.

    Industry observers note that we reached out to textile experts for tips on how to extend the life of leather furniture. Here's how often you should clean and condition these pieces, and how to tell the difference between normal patina and damage that needs attention.

    Industry observers note that lisa Beach is the director of operations at BenchMade Modern, a furniture company that specializes in leather. According to her, cleaning your leather furniture regularly protects it from damage.

    In a recent development, she recommends vacuuming your leather furniture and wiping it down with a dry cloth any time you notice dust, pet hair and dander, or crumbs starting to accumulate. This can range from every one to two weeks, depending on how often you use the furniture. The goal is to prevent these particles from settling into the furniture and possibly scratching the surface.

    In general, she warns against using a damp cloth during these quick and frequent cleanings. "For semi-aniline or protected leathers, you may wipe down your furniture every few months with a damp cloth, but be sure to follow with a dry cloth to remove any excess moisture," she claims. "Natural full-grain leathers are more absorbent, so we don't recommend using damp cloths or moisture unless you need to clean a spill or stain.".

    Leather furniture also benefits from a deeper clean with a specialized pH-balanced product every few months.

    Shawn McGowen is the CEO of Leather Honey, a family-owned organization that has been producing leather care products since 1968. He suggests blocking off time for a deep clean every three to six months, and following it up with a leather conditioner.

    It has been revealed that leather naturally ages and develops a patina over time. McGowen says patinaed leather indicates off a slightly darker color, softer sheen and smoother feel. You'll first notice this starting to develop in the places you sit and rest your arms most often.

    "This is where your natural body oils slowly burnish the leather’s surface, giving that lived-in look that people seek after," he notes. "On the flip side, damage often occurs due to neglect and looks more like cracking, flaking, stiffness, or wrinkling that doesn’t go away with cleaning. Patina comes from properly using your leather while damage comes from neglect.".

    Note that leather furniture can fade instead of darken with age if it sits in a particularly sunny room. However, this doesn't mean you need to keep the curtains drawn or move your leather furniture to a darker corner. McGowen notes that at-home recoloring balms or leather dyes are very easy to apply to small areas.

    Even if you're a very determined DIYer, it's notable to know when it's best to reach out to a leather care professional to restore your furniture. Otherwise, you may end up doing more harm than good.

    Industry observers note that "When leather becomes too far gone and starts to show signs of neglect or wear such as tears, holes, large areas of discoloration, or stains, that is when the DIY becomes more difficult and potentially a waste of time," McGowen notes. "These should often be handled by professional leather care specialists because they have years of experience in color matching and upholstery, and have a wide range of tools needed for larger restoration projects.".

    Follow House Beautiful on Instagram and TikTok.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After quitting architecture school in 1949, Allan Gelbin spent four years working for Frank Lloyd Wright at his Taliesin East studio in Spring Green, Wisconsin.
    • Sources indicate that also making waves this week is the onetime Manhattan studio of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner, the pioneering Abstract Expressionists who are the subject of a new show at The Met.
    • According to recent reports, with its organic silhouette, cantilevered roofline, and clever use of space, Leuthold House by Allan Gelbin bears the hallmarks of his mentor, legendary architect Frank Lloyd Wright.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After quitting architecture school in 1949, Allan Gelbin spent four years working for Frank Lloyd Wright at his Taliesin East studio in Spring Green, Wisconsin. Gelbin later established his own practice in Connecticut, deeply inspired by his time apprenticing under the legendary architect. Now, one of Gelbin’s best-preserved creations—where Wright’s influence is very much clear—has just hit the market: Leuthold House in Newly introduced Canaan is now available for $6.2 million.

    Sources indicate that also making waves this week is the onetime Manhattan studio of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner, the pioneering Abstract Expressionists who are the subject of a new show at The Met. Dolly Parton’s former L.A. home is also for sale, as is Lauren Conrad’s house where much of MTV’s Laguna Beach was filmed. See below for what else caught our eye in the real estate world.

    According to recent reports, with its organic silhouette, cantilevered roofline, and clever use of space, Leuthold House by Allan Gelbin bears the hallmarks of his mentor, legendary architect Frank Lloyd Wright. Completed in 1966 on five rolling acres in Upcoming Canaan, the five-bedroom house spans roughly 5,700 square feet and underwent a restoration by Hobbs Inc. and JMK Architects in 2014. The interiors feature long expanses of glass and mahogany, while the grounds come with a spring-fed pond, a pool, a one-bedroom guest house, and 150 specimen trees. Listed for $6.2 million with John Engel and Melissa Engel of Douglas Elliman, the two-story house is on the market for the first time in 29 years.

    Sources indicate that from a one-bedroom cabin in rural Tennessee to a 63-acre Nashville compound, Dolly Parton’s homes reflected her humble beginnings and subsequent rise to the top of the entertainment industry. In the mid-1980s, a few years after the country music legend starred in her first Hollywood film, 9 to 5, she and her husband Carl Dean bought a property in Southern California. Now, just weeks after Parton’s death at age 80, their Los Angeles estate, which was rebuilt in 2009, according to the listing, just hit the market for $8 million.

    It has been revealed that one of the art world’s most famous couples once lived and worked in a gated townhouse a block from Washington Square Park. Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner didn’t own the MacDougal Alley home—a brick-faced carriage house built in the 1870s—but rather stayed there in the winter of 1950 due to the generosity of its owner, a fellow celebrated artist and their friend Alfonso Ossorio. Now, Ossorio’s 1,500-square-foot residence is on the market for the first time since 1988, per the Newly introduced York Post. The asking price for the two-bedroom, two-bath home is nearly $8 million.

    It’s perhaps the most famous house in one of London’s most charming neighborhoods, so beloved that crowds are known to gather around it like the English version of Carrie Bradshaw’s West Village apartment. It’s the blue-doored townhouse where Hugh Grant’s fictional bookseller lived and wooed Julia Roberts’s paparazzi-plagued Hollywood actress in 1999’s Notting Hill. Despite starring in a blockbuster rom-com, the 2,750-square-foot house in question is very much real—and now it can be yours. That is, for roughly $10 million.

    It has been revealed that this house needs no introduction for fans of MTV’s hit reality show Laguna Beach. The six-bedroom mansion is where series star Lauren “L.C.” Conrad lived with her family, including dad James Conrad, the architect who designed the residence in 2004. Inside the 8,000-square-foot home are travertine floors, wood-beamed ceilings, and stone fireplaces, while the grounds come with an expansive pool court and sweeping Pacific Ocean vistas. When L.C. moved to Los Angeles to star in The Hills, her parents parted with the 11-acre estate, selling it for a reported $11.9 million in 2008. It’s now listed for $26.5 million with Sotheby’s broker Richard Trey Dewey.

    Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

    • The three-bedroom, one-bathroom house was a simple home for someone whose music would change pop culture.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that from the sidewalk, 3137 Whittier Street looks like any other early-20th century home in St. Louis. The red brick exterior, modest size, and simple covered porch don’t hint at its musical past. But this is where Chuck Berry lived in the 1950s, raising his family and creating the sound of rock and roll—a “mixture of a lot of music,” he once told St. Louis Magazine. In this petite house, he wrote songs that would resonate with a global audience and make him one of the most influential musicians of the 20th century.

    According to recent reports, built in 1910, the single-story brick cottage is located in the Greater Ville neighborhood in north St. Louis. Berry and wife Themetta Suggs bought it for $4,500 in 1950, back when he was still trying to make a name for himself as a musician. They lived there with their growing family until 1958.

    The three-bedroom, one-bathroom house was a simple home for someone whose music would change pop culture. In 1956, Berry used his carpentry skills to personalize the house, adding a two-room concrete-block extension at the back. The renovation gave his family more space and provided him with a place to rehearse. He also set up a studio in the basement, where he recorded and worked on songs as his career took off.

    During these years, Berry helped define the rock-and-roll sound, writing records and blending blues, rhythm and blues, and country with his energetic electric guitar style. His hit single “Maybellene,” released in 1955, brought him national attention, followed by popular tracks like “Roll Over Beethoven” (1956), “Rock and Roll Music” (1957), “Sweet Little Sixteen” (1958), and “Johnny B. Goode” (1958).

    Recent findings suggest that berry’s influence reached far beyond his own records. His sharp guitar riffs, driving rhythms, and lyrics created a musical blueprint that inspired generations of performers. The Beatles and the Rolling Stones, for instance, were just some of the British artists who recorded his songs and introduced his music to latest fans, helping cement his legacy on both sides of the Atlantic. In 1986, Berry was inducted into the inaugural class of the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

    The Whittier Street house holds a special place in St. Louis’s Black history. The nearby Ville neighborhood was a cultural hub for Black residents during segregation and home to influential figures in music, sports, and the arts, including Tina Turner, Arthur Ashe, and Josephine Baker. In 2008, Berry’s home was added to the National Register of Historic Places, honoring its connection to his stardom and Black performing arts history.

    It has been revealed that berry died on March 18, 2017, at age 90. But his old home stands as a reminder of the formative years of his groundbreaking career.

    In a recent development, berry’s house isn’t open for tours—most people only catch a glimpse from the street—and few, if any, public interior photos are widely available. But according to St. Louis Realtors, original features like hardwood floors, plaster, doors, and fixtures are still there.

    Recent findings suggest that preservation efforts are at the moment underway to save the house after years of sitting empty and deteriorating. In 2022, the St. Louis Development Corporation made the house a priority project, with goals that include community involvement and future redevelopment. According to a March report, the City of St. Louis has completed initial stabilization work, including floor repairs and masonry restoration.

    According to recent reports, the house’s long-term use is still undecided. But regardless of what it becomes, it stands as a part of history—an ordinary family home that became the backdrop for music that would echo around the world.

    Industry observers note that brea Cubit is an award-winning journalist who covers culture, entertainment, fashion, business, and more. When she’s not writing and editing, she enjoys listening to live music, binge-watching nostalgic TV, and shopping at artisan markets.

    #7959. Before & After: How an Artist and Architect Couple Turned the “Worst House” on the Block Into Their Dream Home

    📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1176 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    Before & After: How an Artist and Architect Couple Turned the “Worst House” on the Block Into Their Dream Home

    📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, before they stepped foot inside the crumbling brownstone on a landmark block in Brooklyn’s Boerum Hill, artist Katherine Keltner and architect Douglas Gauthier had toured 30 homes and browsed more than 200 online.
    • Sources indicate that “This was the first one that had the bones that Katherine wanted,” recalls Gauthier, who runs the firm GAuthier Architects.
    • The strategy paid off: Once their offer was accepted, the couple embarked on an 18-month-long odyssey that saw them jump through a series of hoops (preservationists; concerned neighbors; skeptical engineers) to completely transform the moldering pile into a creative haven for them to live, work, and raise their daughter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, before they stepped foot inside the crumbling brownstone on a landmark block in Brooklyn’s Boerum Hill, artist Katherine Keltner and architect Douglas Gauthier had toured 30 homes and browsed more than 200 online. Neither of them expected to become instantly captivated by the 1869 Italianate townhouse, which was being sold in a stately yet dilapidated condition, having once served as a single-room occupancy (SRO) residence. But it happened nonetheless.

    Sources indicate that “This was the first one that had the bones that Katherine wanted,” recalls Gauthier, who runs the firm GAuthier Architects. “It follows the classic real estate rule of buying the worst house on the best block.”.

    The strategy paid off: Once their offer was accepted, the couple embarked on an 18-month-long odyssey that saw them jump through a series of hoops (preservationists; concerned neighbors; skeptical engineers) to completely transform the moldering pile into a creative haven for them to live, work, and raise their daughter.

    A true joint-effort, Gauthier oversaw a modest two-story rear expansion and structural alterations, while Keltner took charge of spatial arrangements as well as color, pattern, texture, and artwork—much of it her own.

    Sources indicate that once deteriorating, the interiors now have an easy elegance, with plaster walls, arched passageways, and curved corners that give the soaring ceilings an intimate feel. Pink takes an unexpected starring role, appearing throughout the parlor floor and also in the zellige-clad primary bath, but other adventurous hues like mint green and crimson also feature prominently. Capping it off is a plywood-sheathed office for Gauthier’s practice, allowing the family retreat to double as a place of creative inspiration.

    Below, Keltner and Gauthier share their biggest lessons (and some “before” pictures) from the painstaking passion project.

    According to recent reports, when the townhouse was converted to an SRO, it had been chopped up into at least 13 units and two kitchens, and few of the original decorative elements were still intact. A couple had bought it in the 1960s and made it a family home again and added an art gallery space. But by 2021, when Keltner and Gauthier first saw it, the house was in a state of severe neglect, with peeling paint, crumbling floors, ancient appliances—not to mention a 1,500-pound printing press in the studio (that the couple later preserved). Yet, Keltner and Gauthier saw an opportunity, not to recreate the past, but rather forge their own set of rules.

    “The house wasn’t burdened with pristine historic details—our moldings were trashed,” indicates Gauthier. “There were a few things that we kept and celebrated, but to me, it was like a tabula rasa. We can just go in and make it ours.” Katherine agreed: “I feel like sometimes having to preserve things is more expensive than just starting clean,” she says. “And so I thought that was an advantage for us.”.

    According to recent reports, not having to be too precious with ornamentation allowed the couple to make a bold statement about crown moldings, eschewing tradition and installing curving corners and coved ceilings instead. Nowhere does the effect have more impact than in the parlor, where Gauthier devised a ceiling light in the shape of a giant oval that casts light upward rather than down. “I really like indirect lighting,” he notes.

    According to recent reports, crafted out of laser-cut plywood, the elliptical fixture is an abstracted homage to the ceiling medallions found in neighboring historic brownstones. “Some of them are incredibly ornate and beautiful, but they don't really have any use—they’re just decoration,” claims Gauthier. “Adding ambient lighting to the living space takes that historical reference in pocket.”.

    Once they were through the process of changing the structure’s zoning from an SRO to a single-family home, Gauthier and Keltner had to contend with its landmarked status, meaning a series of approvals were required for any additions or exterior modifications.

    The couple originally planned to construct a three-story extension in the back, but they ended up compromising on two floors. This expansion includes a bump-out for the parlor floor’s kitchen, leading to a rear deck that steps down to the garden. On top, a private terrace connects to the primary bath. “Instead of having that third story, we now have a deck off of our primary suite,” claims Keltner. “It’s kind of amazing,” adds Gauthier.

    One decision the couple wrestled with mightily was whether to replace the original, 150-year-old pine flooring with ebony-stained white oak. “The floors were part of the reason we liked the house so much,” notes Gauthier. But their contractor talked them out of keeping them. “It’s a lot of extra work for them,” says Keltner. “They have to take it up, save it, put something else down, and then put it back. I think we reached a point in time and money where we were like, Okay, fine.”.

    Another flooring regret was not adding underfoot heating. “I was pushing the mechanical engineers to do radiant heating and radiant cooling,” indicates Gauthier. “Radiant heat is really lovely—you have warmth under your feet all the time.” But the mechanics behind the system proved complicated and technically redundant, as the home was already configured with a forced-air HVAC system.

    In a recent development, “In doing research and other projects, it’s clear that the cost-to-pleasure ratio would have been worth it,” he states now. “We regret not putting the warm floors in.”.

    According to recent reports, while windows might sometimes be an afterthought, Keltner and Gauthier have advice: Go with triple-glazed. “Windows provide heat and cool insulation as well as security,” explains Keltner. “And they can define both the outside and the inside of a space.” The couple went with triple-glazed windows from Austrian-based firm Bewiso that come pre-wired for easy connection to alarm systems. “They’re almost like hurricane windows,” she claims.

    “You can't break through three panes of glass,” notes Gauthier. Due to the building’s landmark status, they had to use historic-style windows on the front facade. “We were able to get these old-fashioned type of windows that when you close them, they feel like you're closing a Mercedes,” says Gauthier. “They completely silence the outdoors.”.

    The final piece of advice is perhaps the most crucial: “Hire the best contractor you can afford,” says Gauthier.

    Industry observers note that “The typical advice is to get a few bids and throw out the lowest and the highest,” says Keltner. “People usually take the second lowest.” However, that could be the determining factor between an on-time project and one that drags. “You’ll end up paying the difference both in money and time,” she says. “It’s often hard for people to bite the bullet and go with the slightly higher price, but it really pays off.”.

    Recent findings suggest that geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

Mercury and Venus turn direct on the 13th, helping a private concern or friendship question become less tangled. Your season begins on November 22, followed by a Gemini Full Moon in your partnership sector on the 24th. Someone else’s needs may be especially clear, but that does not make yours negotiable by default. With Mars entering your career sector on the 25th, agree on what you can realistically give before work claims the rest .

    Design note: If your home doubles as an office, make it possible to put work away. You shouldn’t have to look at tomorrow’s assignments throughout dinner.

    It has been revealed that november’s opening weeks turn your attention towards friends, collaborators, and plans that require more than your own effort. The Scorpio Newly introduced Moon on the 9th could help you establish a new connection or give an existing project a clearer purpose. When Mercury and Venus turn direct on the 13th, discussions inviting your wider circle and professional direction may start moving again. The Gemini Full Moon on the 24th highlights your workload and routines, making it easier to see what has become unnecessarily complicated. Before accepting another responsibility, consider whether you want it—or whether everyone has simply become accustomed to you saying yes.

    Design note: Retire a household routine that creates more work than it saves.

    In a recent development, the Scorpio Newly introduced Moon on November 9 brings a professional goal into focus. Mercury is still retrograde in that part of your chart until the 13th, so use the early days to refine what you want to say rather than assuming the first version is final. Mid-month, Mars meets Jupiter in your partnership sector, giving a collaboration considerable momentum. It may also make another person’s confidence difficult to distinguish from a workable initiative. Ask practical questions. The Gemini Full Moon on the 24th turns attention towards creativity and enjoyment, reminding you that a personal project does not need a business case to deserve your time.

    Design note: Give an unfinished creative project another chance before clearing it away.

    November begins with an invitation to expand your references. The Scorpio Fresh Moon on the 9th favors study, travel, or a subject that draws you beyond your usual interests. Mercury turning direct there on the 13th helps you return to a plan with better information. Later, the Gemini Full Moon on November 24 lands in your home sector, bringing a domestic matter to a point of clarity. You may recognize that a room, arrangement, or family expectation needs to change. Mars enters your partnership sector the following day, making direct discussion more key—and potentially more heated. State the problem without assigning someone the role of villain.

    Design note: Identify the change you want before discussing how to achieve it.

    The qualifications outlined below serve as a guide to determine if your skills and experience align with the requirements of this position:.

    The Infrastructure team operates and maintains Bloomreach Engagement core infrastructure built on Google Cloud with security, high availability, costs, and scalability in mind. Our vision is to identify and implement opportunities to achieve a robust, reliable, and efficient infrastructure and development platform. We strongly support DevOps culture: each team is responsible for releasing, operating, and monitoring their own applications.

    Sources indicate that the role of the Infrastructure Team is to provide a strong foundation upon which all teams can build, for example, manage big infrastructure components like Kubernetes, databases, and cloud components in Google Cloud. An important role of the team is also to provide support to developers, review design proposals, validate the performance and availability of applications, and sometimes even develop latest core application components such as logging or authorization.

    In the position of Staff DevOps Engineer, you’d be expected to work with other Engineering teams to design sustainable infrastructure, microservice solutions, and an efficient and robust production environment. Additionally, you’ll be working on a variety of tasks and projects, including automating tools and infrastructure to reduce manual work, monitoring applications and participating in an on-call rotation as required.

    It has been revealed that you’ll own the design and specification of infrastructure initiatives, break them down into tasks the team can execute, and lead projects that span multiple engineering teams. AI assistants are a given part of your toolkit, and you retain full understanding of, and responsibility for, what gets shipped.

    The ideal candidate will be passionate about learning fresh things, creative, willing to take the initiative, and able to think outside the box to solve problems strategically.

    (*Subject to employment type. Interns are exempt from marked benefits, usually for the first 6 months.).
